build: cartridge image, CBM80 header at $8004, cold start $9593

extra: pre-shifted byte tables the blitter uses instead of shifting at run time
cartridge header, shape pointer table and shape bitmaps

comments.text: 6510 data direction register. The game never writes it; the loader leaves the KERNAL's $2F here, which makes bits 0-5 outputs so that the bank bits in $01 work. Listed only because the disassembler mints a symbol for it.

6510 processor port. The game runs with $36 here (BASIC ROM out, I/O in, KERNAL in), set by the loader before it jumps to $9593. The only code that touches it is the character-set copy at $BFA2-$BFCF, which clears bit 2 (CHAREN) so the character ROM appears at $D000, copies $D000-$D7FF to $5000-$57FF, and sets bit 2 again.

Non-zero while one of the five centred messages ($8A8B) is on screen: $8A97 leaves the message pointer's high byte here and $8AC7 leaves 0 when it wipes the message. The raster handler at $9A85 adds it to $93 and, if the sum is zero, skips the mid-screen text window and sets the next raster interrupt to line $E0 instead of $81. Also cleared at $95EB and by the cold start at $BF08.

Bitmap row of the first row of the shape being drawn, counted upward from the bottom of the play area (0-167), i.e. an index into the row-address tables at $0A00/$0AA8. $8B91 loads it from the third byte of the caller's parameter block; $8C6A and $8E7A copy it into the working row $31 and $90EF into $0B.

Low byte of the 16-bit X of the shape being drawn, in bitmap pixels. $8B91 loads $04/$05 from the first two bytes of the caller's parameter block. $8DD0 splits the pair into a byte column ($08) and a bit position ($09); $8C89, $8EB4, $9115 and $9173 add this byte masked with $F8 to a row address to reach the bitmap byte to write.

High byte of the 16-bit draw X whose low byte is $04. $8DD8-$8DE0 shifts $05:$04 right three times to produce the byte column in $08, restoring the pair from $12/$13 afterwards; $8C99, $8EC2, $9123 and $9181 add it to the high byte of the row address.

Pointer to the bitmap byte the blitter is writing. Built at $8C84-$8C9B, $8EAF-$8EC4, $9110-$9125 and $916E-$9183 from the row-address tables plus the byte column, with $0F eored into the high byte to pick the buffer; $9000-$90AD and $915A read-modify-write through it. The same pair doubles as the message-string pointer in $8A90-$8AB8 and as the star address in $9228-$9248.

High byte of the bitmap write pointer in $06: a row-table high byte plus $05 with the double-buffer bit from $0F already folded in, so it points into $2000-$3F3F or $6000-$7F3F. Written at $8C9B, $8D59, $8D71, $8EC4, $9125, $9183 and $9237.

X of the shape being drawn in whole bitmap bytes (draw X >> 3), computed by $8DD0. $8C6F-$8C7C clamps a horizontal bar so that this column plus the width does not run past column 40; $9135 uses it to measure how far a sheared line has moved, and $920F/$921C step it when the pixel mask falls out of its byte.

Bit position of the draw X inside its byte. $8DD0 leaves 8 minus (X and 7) here and $8DBE turns that count into a single-bit mask; $9207 and $9214 rotate the mask when a sheared line moves one pixel sideways, carrying into the byte column $08.
Blitter scratch: the shape byte after it has been shifted into position, saved by $8E96 and re-read at $900B, $9028, $908C and $90A7 so the same value can be ored into two adjacent bitmap bytes.
Row counter of the sheared-line drawer at $90E9-$91FA: $90EF copies the starting row from $03, $910C reloads it into $31 at the top of each row and $91F4 decrements it once per shape row.

Blitter column state. In the flat blitter ($8EA0, $9077, $9088) it is the number of shifts still to apply to the current shape byte; in the sheared drawer ($9144-$91BF) it is the single-bit pixel mask, rotated left or right according to bit 7 of $2F and reset to $80 or $01 when it falls out of the byte.

Offset from the row base to the bitmap byte currently being written, used as the index in sta ($06),y. $8E9A clears it, $9011 and $90B8 step it by a row, $913A sets it from the difference between two byte columns, and $91B1/$91C4 move it by eight when the sheared drawer changes byte column.
Width counter of the blitter's inner loop: $8E92 and $9148 load it with the (clipped) shape width from $10 and $9019, $9081 and $91C8 count it down to zero, one pixel per pass.

Double-buffer selector: 0 while bank 0 (matrix $0400, bitmap $2000) is the drawing target, $40 while bank 1 (matrix $4400, bitmap $6000) is. $8D0F clears it, $8D16 flips it with eor #$40 and $8D1F writes the matching VIC bank number into $DD00. Every row-address high byte is eored with it ($8C97, $8EC0, $9121, $917F, $9235), which is what puts the two bitmaps exactly $4000 apart.

Width in bitmap bits of the shape being drawn, read from the shape's first header byte by $8EEE or $8F0D. $8E68 subtracts the left and right clip counts ($22, $23) from it, $8DF3 rounds it up to whole bytes into $2A, and $8E92/$9148 copy it into the inner-loop counter $0E.

Height in rows of the shape being drawn, read from the shape's second header byte by $8EF3 or $8F12. $8E71 subtracts the top and bottom clip counts ($24, $25); $8CD0, $902E, $90AF and $91EA count it down, one pass per shape row.

Low byte of the general 16-bit scratch pair used all over the drawing code: $8DC8 and $8D98 park a copy of the draw X here while $8DD0 destroys the original, $8CAC holds one of the two bytes the horizontal-bar drawer alternates into the bitmap, and $8E0F collects the low half of the product of the row length by the top clip count.

High half of the $12/$13 scratch pair: the saved high byte of the draw X ($8DCE, $8D9E), the second of the two bytes the bar drawer alternates ($8CC4), and the high half of the shape-data offset that $8E1F adds to the shape pointer $17/$18.

General byte scratch of the drawing and message code: the count of characters still to print in $8AAB-$8AC2, the run length of a horizontal bar in $8D44-$8D4D, and the low byte of the clip-offset multiply at $8E01-$8E39.
Row counter of the horizontal-bar drawer ($8D4B, $8D78) and of the tall-shape loop at $9057-$9069; $912B-$9142 also uses it to remember the byte column across a call to $8DC8.

The shape byte currently being unpacked, shifted left one bit per pixel by $8EAB and $9152 so that bit 7 is always the next pixel; $91E5 reloads it from the next shape byte every eight pixels and $9150 primes it in the sheared drawer.

Pointer into the shape being drawn, and the inline-argument pointer of the $8B1E/$8B38 convention. $8B2A and $8B53 load it with the caller's return address, or with the word that address points at, so the two bytes after the jsr can be read; afterwards $8EE2 and the blitters walk it through the shape bitmap, $8E1B, $8EDB and $91DB advancing it. $8BDD resumes the caller with jmp ($17).
High byte of the shape / inline-argument pointer in $17. Written at $8B2D, $8B58, $8BD7, $8E21, $8E64, $8E8A and $8EE8, and carried into at $8B33, $8EDF and $91DF.

Blitter scratch used only by the wide-shape path at $8FF6-$90AB: $8FF6 stores the byte fetched from the shape, $907C rotates it right into carry, and $9090 and $90AB or it into the bitmap byte being assembled. $90A2 shifts it again for the second of the two bytes a shifted shape spans.

Bit counter of the sheared-line drawer, 0 to 7: $914C clears it, $91CC increments it once per pixel and $91D0 tests it against 8, at which point $91DB steps the shape pointer $17/$18 on to the next byte and $91E3 refills $16. Its span also covers $1B when nothing else claims it.

Return address of a routine that takes an inline pointer. $8B38 pops the caller's return address into $1B/$1C, reads the two-byte pointer that follows the jsr into $17/$18, steps $1B past it, and hands control back with jmp ($1B) from $8BAC, $8BF6, $8C14 and $8C2D.
High byte of the inline-argument return address in $1B, incremented at $8B4D when the pop carries and at $8B63 when stepping past the inline word.

Saved accumulator. Every routine that must not disturb the caller's registers stores A here on entry ($8B91, $8BBA, $8BE0, $8BF9, $8C17, $8C5E, $8F03, $8FD3, $903E, $90D2) and reloads it just before the rts ($8BA8, $8CD9, $8FCC, $9037, $90CB, $9221).
Saved X register, companion of $1D. Written on entry at $8C32, $8C60, $8F05, $8FD5, $9040 and $90D4 and restored at $8C45, $8CDB, $8FCE, $9039, $90CD and $9223.

Saved Y register, the third of the $1D/$1E/$1F save area. Written on entry to all the inline-argument routines ($8B93, $8BBC, $8BE2, $8BFB, $8C19) and to the shape drawers, and reloaded immediately before they return.

Two jobs. In $8B1E and $8B38 it is the resume vector: the caller's return address plus one, jumped through by jmp ($20) at $8B35 and $8B65 once the inline argument has been read. In the horizontal-bar drawer it is a second copy of the bitmap pointer $06/$07 ($8C92, $8C9D) that $8CC6 writes the alternate colour byte through.
High byte of the $20/$21 resume vector, written at $8B27 and $8B41, and of the bar drawer's second bitmap pointer, written at $8C9D.

Pixels clipped off the left edge of the shape being drawn. $8CFE zeroes it before every shape and the clipper at $8F35-$8F4E sets it when the shape starts left of the window. $8E23-$8E39 splits it into a whole-byte offset ($27) and a shift ($26) and $8E6B subtracts it from the width.
Pixels clipped off the right edge of the shape. Zeroed by $8CFE, set at $8F95, and subtracted from the width together with $22 at $8E6D.

Rows clipped off the top of the shape. Zeroed by $8CFE, set at $8FAA. $8DFD-$8E21 multiplies it by the bytes-per-row in $2A and adds the product to the shape pointer so drawing starts at the first visible row; $8E74 subtracts it from the height.
Rows clipped off the bottom of the shape. Zeroed by $8CFE, set by $8BAF (which also clears $22-$24) and by $8FC9, and subtracted from the height at $8E76.

Eight minus the left-clip remainder ($22 and 7), computed at $8E35. $8E9E-$8EA4 uses it as the number of left shifts applied to the first shape byte of each row so the clipped-off pixels fall out of the byte.

Left clip in whole shape bytes ($22 >> 3), computed at $8E28 and added to the shape pointer at $8E5A. $8E43 bumps it by one when the shape has to be nudged a whole byte, and $8EC6 tests it to decide whether a partial byte from before the row start has to be fetched.

Running pointer to the start of the shape row being drawn. $8E5E/$8E66 set it from $17/$18 once the clipping offsets are folded in, and $8E7F-$8E8E copies it into $17/$18 and then advances it by one row ($2A bytes) ready for the next pass.
High byte of the shape-row pointer in $28, set at $8E66 and carried at $8E8C; $8E88 reloads it into $18 at the top of each row.

Bytes per row of the shape being drawn, ($10 + 7) >> 3, computed at $8DF3-$8DFB. $8E0C uses it as the multiplicand when skipping clipped rows and $8E84 adds it to the row pointer $28/$29 once per row.

Run length of the slope used by the sheared drawer at $90E9: the number of pixel columns to cover before stepping one bitmap row. $8C30 looks it up, together with $2C, in the eleven-entry table at $8C48 from a slope index of -5..+5; the values are 0, 3, 4, 5, 10 and 13. $9104, $9162 and $91FD reload the counters $30, $32 and $33 from it.

Row step of the slope used by the sheared drawer: $01 to climb a row, $FF to drop one, $00 for a flat run. Set with $2B by $8C30 from the table at $8C48. $9169 adds it to the working row $31, $9186 to the running total $33, and $9201 eors it with $2F to decide which way the pixel mask moves.
Cleared to zero by $8CE0 along with the rest of the drawing state. No instruction anywhere in $8000-$BFFF reads it; purpose unknown.
Cleared to zero by $8CE0 with the rest of the drawing state. Like $2D it is written once and never read in $8000-$BFFF; purpose unknown.

Direction flag for the drawing code, tested with bit at $8DA0, $91A3 and $9203 and written only at $90DA. When bit 7 is set the shape is laid down right to left: $8DA7 biases the start X by the width and the pixel mask in $0C is rotated the other way.
Outer run counter of the sheared drawer: $90F3 loads it from $2B and $91F6 decrements it once per shape row; at zero $91FD reloads it and $9207/$9214 move the pixel mask on by one.

Bitmap row the drawing code is working on, used as the index into the row-address tables at $0A00/$0AA8. $8C6A and $8E7C load it from $03, $8CD4 walks it down one row per pass of the bar drawer, $910E reloads it from $0B, and $9167-$916B adds the slope step $2C to it.
Inner run counter of the sheared drawer, reloaded from $2B at $9104 and $9164 and decremented at $915E for every pixel column; reaching zero triggers the row step.

Running row position of the sheared drawer, reloaded from $2B at $9106 and advanced by the slope step $2C at $9186; $918E and $9195/$919C fold it back into range so the shear stays inside the run length.

First byte of the three-byte inline argument fetched by $8BF9 from the block the caller names after the jsr. With $35 it is a 16-bit world X that the clipper at $8F1F-$8F3E compares with the window origin $3B/$3C to work out how much of the shape falls off the left or right edge. Callers pass the address $0067 ($9DFA, $A0C4, $AA9E, $B74B, $B8E5, $BA62), so in practice $34/$35/$36 is a copy of $67/$68/$69.
High byte of the 16-bit position in $34, fetched by $8BF9. $8F19 compares it with $3C and $8F2E/$8F3E subtract it when the clipper measures the horizontal overlap.
Third byte of the $8BF9 inline argument: the bitmap row the shape is to be drawn at. $8F97-$8FB7 compares it with the clip bounds $39 and $3A to produce the top and bottom clip counts $24 and $25.

Pointer to the shape being drawn. It is the two-byte inline argument of $8BBA (which takes the value itself) and of $8BE0 (which takes the address of the value). $8EE2 copies it into $17/$18 and reads the width and height header bytes through it; $8F0B/$8F10 read the same two bytes directly.
High byte of the shape pointer in $37, written by $8BCA and $8BF0 and read at $8EE6.

Highest bitmap row the drawing code may touch. $8CE0 sets it to $A7 (167), the top row of the 168-row play area, and the vertical clipper at $8F9B-$8FAC subtracts the shape's row from it to get the top clip count $24.
Lowest bitmap row the drawing code may touch, set to 0 by $8CE0. $8C80 stops the horizontal-bar drawer when the row index falls below it, and $8FBB uses it to work out the bottom clip count $25.

World X of the left edge of the drawing window, the two-byte inline argument of $8C17. Zeroed by $8CE0; the only callers, $9741 and $BDCB, pass the address $0075, so it is normally a copy of the view origin $75/$76. The clipper at $8F21-$8F3C subtracts it from the shape's world X in $34/$35 to get the position relative to the window and the left and right clip counts.
High byte of the drawing-window origin in $3B, set at $8C27 and cleared at $8CF4 and compared with $35 at $8F19. Its span also covers $3D and $3E, which no instruction in $8000-$BFFF touches.
Cleared to zero by $8CE0 with the rest of the drawing state and never read anywhere in $8000-$BFFF; purpose unknown. Its span also covers $40, which nothing touches.

Carry byte of the pixel shifter: the bits pushed out of the previous shape byte, which $9003/$9008 or into the next byte before it is written. $8E98 clears it at the start of a row and $8ED9 primes it from the byte before the first visible one when the shape is clipped on the left.
Low byte, always zero ($8D09), of the shift-right lookup pointer whose high byte is $43. $9001 reads a shifted byte through it out of the tables the cold start builds at $1000-$17FF.

High byte of the shift-right lookup pointer $42/$43. $8E50 sets it to $10 ored with the shift count 0-7, so lda ($42),y yields y >> shift. The eight 256-byte tables at $1000-$17FF are built by the loop at $BF63-$BF98.
Low byte, always zero ($8D0B), of the shift-out lookup pointer whose high byte is $45. $8ED7 and $9006 read through it to get the bits a right shift pushes out of a byte.

High byte of the shift-out lookup pointer $44/$45. $8E55 sets it to $18 ored with the shift count, so lda ($44),y yields y << (8 - shift), from the eight tables the cold start builds at $1800-$1FFF. Its span also covers $46-$50, which nothing in $8000-$BFFF touches.

Zeroed by the per-sortie reset at $BED9. Read and written only by the landscape and scroll code: $A421-$A425, $A43F-$A456 and $A696 add to it, $A52B/$A556/$A640 read it, and $BD18/$BDD1 copy it into $7F as the low half of a 16-bit value handed to the shift routine $ACF1. It behaves as the low byte of a signed 16-bit quantity paired with $52; the quantity itself is not established.

High half of the pair that starts at $51, zeroed at $BEDB. As well as the arithmetic at $A427-$A45D it is used as a flag: $9F2D, $9FF5, $A07C, $A49A, $A839, $BCB0, $BCB7, $BD32 and $BD55 all branch on bit 7, and $A527 eors it. $BCAA-$BCB9 combines its sign with the helicopter facing $59 to decide which way the view should scroll. Exact meaning not established.

Zeroed at $BEDD. Used only inside the landscape code at $A48E-$A6CD: $A570 and $A580 subtract and add it in a 16-bit sum with $54, and $A5D6, $A60A and $A6CD rewrite it. Exact meaning not established.
Zeroed at $BEDF, the companion of $53. $A469/$A488 use it in the same 16-bit sum, $A4F6 and $A5EB test bit 7, and $A5DE/$A610/$A6CF rewrite it. Exact meaning not established.

Low byte of a 16-bit world X that the per-sortie reset $BEE1-$BEE7 sets to $1273 and that $A62B-$A692 and $A901-$A90B move. Everything that owns a world X subtracts this pair from it to get a position relative to it: the people scan ($9BFC, $9C36, $9CB5), the actor code ($A145, $AEB8, $B448, $B489, $B4CB, $B78F) and the scroll code ($BCCD, $BD06, $BD26), which keeps the view origin $75/$76 within $46 to $FA pixels of it.

High byte of the 16-bit world X in $55, set to $12 by $BEE7. $A633 and $A63E step it when the low byte wraps and every world-to-view subtraction ($9B8F, $9C01, $9F15, $A047, $B19F, $B44F, $B798) uses it as the high half.

Set to 7 by the per-sortie reset at $BEEB. $A6B0-$A6C9 compares and rewrites it, $A915 adds to it, and the actor code reads it at $9FB5, $A154, $AFE3, $B03E and subtracts it at $AE77, $B439, $B47A, $B79F. In the analysed snapshot it always equals the helicopter's +6 field, so it looks like the player's height above the ground, but nothing in the code proves that.

The row the ground sits on, set to $16 (22) by $BEEF and never changed afterwards. $AA06 gives the helicopter the same value in its +7 field when the actor list is built; $B349 and $B4BB test an actor's +7 against it to ask whether that actor is standing on the ground, $B393 subtracts it, and $B6B0/$B714/$B864 copy it into the +7 field of newly spawned actors.

The helicopter's current facing, a small signed number that the per-sortie reset $BEB7 sets to 3. $986C steps it one notch per frame towards a target: +3 or -3 when the joystick is asking for a turn ($8A), otherwise the value the eleven-entry table at $98B0 gives for $5A + 5. $989C and $98A7 make it step past 0 while a turn is being asked for. The shape drawn for the helicopter is chosen from it at $AB5E, $ABE2, $AC4A, $ACCC, $AD26 and $AD6A, and $BCAA uses its sign to pick the scroll direction.

Zeroed by $BEC4. $A628 and $A638 move it by one in step with the world X $55/$56, and $986C indexes the auto-level table at $98B0 with $5A + 5, so it holds a small signed value that tracks the helicopter's horizontal motion; $AB79 and $AC14 pass it to $8C30 as a slope index, and $A92C adds $6D to it. The unit is not established.

Signed horizontal thrust taken from the joystick by $A741: $05 when the stick is pushed left, $FB (-5) when it is pushed right, 0 otherwise, from the four-entry table at $A758. Forced to 0 while the end-of-sortie delay $63 is running and by $9710 during the end screen. Read at $A42D, $A438 and $A616.

Vertical thrust taken from the joystick by $A71A: 15 with the stick up, 5 with it down, 10 with it centred and 0 with both pressed, from the table at $A73D. Forced to 2 while $61 or $63 is non-zero and by $970C on the end screen. Read at $A463.

Zeroed by $BECA and set at $A7FD and $A80C. It drives the rotor pitch: $997A makes the voice-1 frequency in $0B5E climb towards $C0 while it is non-zero and fall towards $30 while it is zero. The control routines also test it first and refuse to fire ($97D2) or to turn ($97F1) when it is zero, and $9C08, $9C23, $A4CA, $A724, $AFB0, $B055, $B4C3 and $BCA6 branch on it. The exact condition that sets it is outside this range.

Set to 1 by $BEBD and rewritten at $A800, $A8B0 and $A8B5. Read at only two places, $9C93 and $9DBD, both inside the people scan $9B7D, where a zero value makes the person's record be marked dead with $FF. Meaning not established.

Set to 1 by $BEBF and rewritten at $A802 and $A829. Read at $9C27, $9E2D and $9E97 in the people scan and at $BCA2, where a non-zero value makes the scroll code advance the view origin by a fixed 4 pixels instead of tracking the helicopter. Meaning not established.
Zeroed by $BECE, written at $A4E7 and $A50D, read at $A4DA, $A7DC, $AB11 and $AB1C. Confined to the landscape and helicopter-drawing code; meaning not established.

Zeroed by $BED0 and set at $A8A7 and $B5B1 (the latter when an actor collides). While it is non-zero the fire button and the turn controls are ignored ($97D8, $97F7), the joystick thrusts are overridden ($A72F) and $9BED, $9C97, $A185, $A1AC, $A1C8, $A5C7, $AE9E and $B04E take a different path. It behaves as 'the helicopter is no longer under the player's control', but what clears it again is outside this range.

Zeroed by $BECC; $A883 decrements it and $A88B and $A8A0 increment it. Read at $A7BF (where the value 6 suppresses a sound effect), $A82B, $A875, $ABB0, $AC19, $AC79, $AFE5 and $B13E. A small counter in the helicopter code; meaning not established.

Zeroed by $BED2 and set at $A87B/$A881. Once non-zero the main loop at $968E adds 3 to it every frame and, when the sum goes negative, abandons the sortie and jumps back to $961E to print the next sortie message. $A733 and $A74E freeze the joystick thrusts $5B and $5C while it runs.

Fire-button latch. $97E7 sets it to $FF at the moment the player's shot is created and $B00A rewrites it; $97DA and $B004 test bit 7. It is what stops one press of the button producing more than one shot.

Pointer to a shape's header, taken from the shape-pointer table at $8009 (or $8091/$8097/$809B) and stored by $9D72, $AB26, $AB37, $AB4F, $AB6C, $AC36, $AC96, $ADD0, $B063, $B116, $B8F5 and $BB10. $AB92, $ADDE, $B071, $B124 then read the width and height bytes through it, and $8BE0 is usually handed the address $0065 so the drawing code picks the same shape up.
High byte of the shape-header pointer in $65, written at $9D77, $9D91, $9DAC, $A119, $AB2B, $AB3C, $AB55, $AB71, $AC3C, $AC9B, $ADD5, $B068, $B11B, $B8FA and $BB15.

Low byte of the world X of the shape about to be queued for drawing. $A9A0 fills $67/$68/$69 from an actor's record: the 16-bit world X in +4/+5 minus the signed X offset the caller passes in the X register ($7B), and the row from +6 plus +7 plus the Y offset in the Y register ($7C). $AA3B then subtracts the view origin $75/$76 and appends the result to the display list; $8BF9 is usually handed the address $0067.
High byte of the world X in $67. $A9B9/$A9C0 set it with the sign of the X offset $7B taken into account; $9DE7, $AA8D, $B8DF, $BA13 and $BA55 write it directly and $AA41 subtracts $76 from it.

Bitmap row of the shape about to be queued, computed at $A9C3-$A9CB as the actor's height above the ground (+6) plus its ground row (+7) plus the caller's Y offset $7C. Also written directly at $9DF8, $AA91, $B8E3, $B90B, $B921, $B935, $BA18, $BA60, $BAA7 and $BADD for scenery that has no actor record.

Low byte of the view-relative X of the display-list entry being built or replayed. $AA3B-$AA3F computes it as $67 minus the view origin $75; $BC0C reads it back out of the previous frame's list, $BC2C-$BC30 and $BC41-$BC56 clip it against the left edge of the screen, and $8B91 is handed the address $006A so it lands in $04.

High byte of the view-relative X of a display-list entry, computed at $AA41-$AA45 and read back at $BC0F. $BC34 decrements it and $BC3D tests its sign when the entry has to be clipped against the left edge.

Bitmap row of a display-list entry, computed at $AA48-$AA4C and read back at $BC14. $BC37 adds 14 to it for entries of kind 0, and $BC60-$BC7A clips it against the 168-row play area, trimming the stored height in $0B52 to match.

The most-used scratch byte in the program (101 references), normally paired with $6E. It serves as a working register for the sound code ($95F9, $9930), the raster handler's screen pointer ($9AD5), the landscape and helicopter code ($A5F1-$A61A, $AB7D, $ACBC, $AD32), the actor-list scan ($B3AD, $B573), the display-list clipper ($BC4B-$BC73), the scroll limiter ($BCD1-$BD4D) and the cold start's bit shifter ($BF7B-$BF8B) and block copies ($BFB2-$BFEF). Nothing keeps a value in it across a routine.

High half of the $6D scratch pair, used the same way: the high byte of the copy pointers in $BFB6-$BFC5 and $BFE7, the quotient in the halving at $AA6A-$AA7C, and the high byte of the distance the scroll code measures at $BCD7-$BD5D.

General 16-bit scratch, and an indirect jump vector: $B319-$B326 puts an actor handler's address here and jumps through it. Also the source pointer of the character-ROM copy at $BFA8-$BFBA and of the bitmap clear at $BFD9-$BFED, the table pointer read at $9AE3 and $ADA6-$ADD3, the destination of the shift tables at $BF67-$BF89, and a plain temporary in a dozen other routines.

High byte of the $6F pair. $BE71 and $BEAB/$BEAF carry the world X through it while the eight people are seeded, $B99E/$B9AB count down with it, and $BFAE/$BFC1 walk it across the character ROM from $D0 to $D7 while $BFDF/$BFF6 walk it across the bitmap from $20 to $3F.

The kind byte of a display-list entry. $AA38 takes it in A and stores it as the first of the four bytes; $BC07/$BC19/$BC27 reads it back when the entry is replayed and uses it to index the offset table at $94AF. $BE75-$BE8E also uses this byte as the counter that seeds the eight people at $0CA0.

Byte offset of the actor record currently being worked on, i.e. ten times the slot number. $B30A sets it as $B307 walks the linked list, the allocator $A951 and the unlinker $A937 pass it, and about eighty sites do ldx $72 followed by lda $0B74,x and friends to reach the record fields.

Zeroed by $B30F at the top of every pass over the actor list and written once, by $A95B, which records the slot offset of the first actor linked in during that pass ($A971 stops a later link overwriting it). No instruction in $8000-$BFFF reads it; purpose unknown.

Head of the free-slot chain of the actor array: the byte offset of the first unused record, or 0 for none. $AA13 sets it to 20 (slot 2) when the list is built, $A951 pops a record off it when an actor is spawned and $A94E pushes a freed record back on. The chain runs through each record's +9 field.

Low byte of the world X of the left edge of the view. $AA3D and $AA43 subtract $75/$76 from a shape's world X to get its screen X, and the scroll code at $BCBF-$BDC9 advances the pair, clamping it between $02B0 and $11D8. $9739 forces it to $11D8 for the frames drawn between phases, and $9741/$BDCB hand its address to $8C17 so the clipper's window origin $3B/$3C is the same value.

High byte of the view origin in $75, set to $11 by $973D. $BCC7, $BD7B and $BD9A step it as the view crosses a 256-pixel boundary, and $B8AF, $B972 and $BA40 compare it with fixed values to decide whether the base, the hangar or the far buildings are close enough to be worth drawing.

Written at $9D59, $A461, $A474, $B67C and $B71C and only ever tested with bit ($A481, $B6BA, $B720), so only its top bits matter to the code that reads it: $B6B8 and $B71E use its sign to flip the sign of a newly spawned actor's +1 field. Meaning not established.

Low byte of a 16-bit working position. $B66D and $B98D set it, $B690, $BA58, $BA74, $BA92, $BAAA and $BAE0 read it and $B9BF-$BA01 add to it repeatedly. It is the anchor X of the routines that draw the hangar ($B971-$BA3A) and the base ($BA3F-$BB24) and the pair used when an actor splits in two at $B665.
High byte of the 16-bit working position in $78, written at $B672 and $B991 and added to at $B9C6, $B9DC, $B9F2 and $BA01.

Written once at $B677 and read twice at $B6A1 and $B6A9, all inside $B665: it holds the +6 field of the actor that is splitting so the two halves can be placed eight rows above and nine rows below it. Purely local.

The signed X offset a caller passes to $A9A0 in the X register: $A9AC subtracts it from the actor's world X and $A9B3 sign-extends it into the high byte, so one actor can queue several shapes at fixed offsets. $BC1D-$BC20 reuses the byte as the width of a display-list entry read from the table at $94AF, and $BC4E-$BC52 trims that width when the entry is clipped on the left.

The signed row offset a caller passes to $A9A0 in the Y register, added to the row at $A9C9. $BC22-$BC25 reuses the byte as the height of a display-list entry, taken from the table at $94B0, and $BC5A copies it into $0B52 for the clip.

Scratch of the scroll code only: $BDEA sets it to the step the view is allowed to move this frame (at least 4, capped at the remaining distance by $BE0E-$BE1A), and $BD75/$BD94 add or subtract it from the view origin $75/$76.

Never referenced by any instruction in $8000-$BFFF. It sits between the scroll scratch $7D and the 16-bit scratch pair $7F/$80 and is left over from the way the zero page is laid out; the game does not use it.

Low byte of a general 16-bit scratch pair used by the landscape, scroll and helicopter code (55 references), and an indirect jump vector at $ABBB. $A56E-$A588, $A5D0-$A5E9 and $A642-$A656 use it as an accumulator, $AA78-$AA8B holds a halved view origin in it, and $BD1A/$BDD3 load it from $51/$52 before calling the shift routine $ACF1.

High half of the $7F scratch pair. $AD07 and $AD1B shift it, $A8FE and $AD21 increment it, $BDF9 tests bit 7 to take the absolute value of the pair, and $BE10 tests it for zero when the scroll step is capped.

Written at $A14A, $A175, $A194 and $B794, tested with bit at $A17A, $A181, $A263 and $A26A and compared at $A1BD and $A223. At $B794 it is the low byte of the world X of the player minus this actor, so in that routine it is a relative position; the earlier uses at $A10A-$A2C0 are not established.

Written at $A151 and $B79B, read at $A15B, $A171, $B7A4 and $B7B6. At $B79B it is the high byte of the world X of the player relative to this actor, and $B7A6-$B7AC uses it to drop an actor that has drifted more than three pages away. The uses in $A151-$A171 are not established.

Written at $A159 and $B7A2 and tested with bit at $B7E6. At $B7A2 it is the height of the player relative to this actor, and its sign decides whether the actor's +2 field counts up or down. The use at $A159 is not established.
Saved X register around the sound, status-bar and actor calls: $A3BA, $A3D3, $A3EC, $A6D2 and $B0D2 push the pair $84/$85 and $A3CE, $A3E7, $A40E, $A6E0, $A715 and $B101 restore it.
Saved Y register, the other half of the $84/$85 register save area; written at $A3BC, $A3D5, $A3EE, $A6D4 and $B0D4 and restored at $A3D0, $A3E9, $A410, $A6E2, $A717 and $B103.

Low byte of a 16-bit temporary of the helicopter and shape code: $ABEE, $AC65, $AC72 and $ADAE set it, $AC07 adds to it, $ACA2 loads it into X, and $AE40-$AE51 steps and tests it. $B01D/$B024 reuses it alone when a shot is created.
High byte of the $86/$87 temporary ($ABF3, $AC6A, $AC77, $ADB3, $AE2D), and on its own the saved height of the shot being checked against the actor list at $B384-$B39A.

Written at $ADB8 and $B555 and read at $AE36 and $B562. At $B555 it holds the +7 field of the actor being tested so the scan at $B55E can reject actors more than ten rows away; the use at $ADB8 is a local temporary of the helicopter drawer.

Frame counter within the current phase. The main loop increments it once per drawn frame ($95C6, $9640, $966F, $96FC) and clears it when a phase starts ($9638, $96EF). $9644 ends the sortie message after $2C frames and $9700 ends the closing screen after $50; $A363, $A36C, $B75F, $B951 and $BB07 take its low bit to alternate animation frames.

The turn the player is asking for this frame: $01 one way, $FF the other, $00 for none. $982F, $9836, $985B, $9864 and $9869 set it from the joystick and the per-sortie reset $BEBB starts it at 1. $986C is the only reader: it turns the request into a one-notch step of the helicopter facing $59.

Remembers the facing the helicopter had when the current turn began: $9826 copies $59 into it and $9814 clears it, and $9851-$9857 compares it with the current facing when the stick is released to decide which way to level off. Zeroed by the per-sortie reset at $BEC2.

Non-zero while the status panel is live. $95AD clears it for the title display, $95F2 sets it to $FF for play and $96F4 clears it again for the closing screen. $A978 and $BB2B refuse to redraw the panel and $A7BB refuses to start a sound effect while it is clear.

Cleared by the panel reset at $BB98 and incremented at $9EBA. $9FD7 uses it as a Y index and $A398/$A3A5 as an X index into the hostage bookkeeping; $B822 compares it with 3 before an actor is allowed to spawn another. It counts something about the hostages the helicopter is carrying, but the exact quantity is not established.

Loop counter of the two table builders in the cold start. $BF38 sets it to 21, one per character row, while $BF3B-$BF61 fills the bitmap row-address tables at $0A00 and $0AA8; $BF65-$BF94 then reuses it as the shift count 0-7 while the sixteen lookup tables at $1000-$1FFF are built. The code addresses it absolutely, which is why the disassembler names it a_008E.

Low byte of the cold start's output pointer. $BF2C holds the running low byte of the bitmap row addresses while $BF3B-$BF61 fills $0A00/$0AA8, and $BF69/$BF8D then points the pair at $1800+n*256 while the shift-out tables are built. $9AD3/$9AE9 reuse it in the raster handler as a screen write pointer.

High byte of the $8F pointer pair. $BF33 starts it at $25 and $BF5B advances it one page per character row (plus the carry out of the $39 added to the low byte), which is how the row addresses step by 320 bytes; $BF77 then points it at page $18+n for the shift-out tables.

Selects how tall the mid-screen text window is. $BF0A clears it, $9AAC and $9B58 set it to 1. In the raster handler $99C4 tests it to choose the raster line that closes the window, $91 (two text rows) when it is zero and $A9 (four rows) when it is not; $9A88 adds it to $02 to decide whether the window is opened at all.

Reload value for the voice-2 retrigger counter $95. $A786 sets it when a sound effect starts and $9A5A copies it back into $95 each time the counter expires; $9985 and $9993 walk it up and down as the note slides.

Counts raster frames until voice 2 is retriggered: $9A4C decrements it in the raster handler and at zero $9A50-$9A57 gates voice 2 off and on again before reloading from $94. $966D sets it to $11 for the between-sorties display and $99A5 to $FF when the effect stops.

Frames since the fire button last changed state. $9A35 increments it once per frame at raster $1E; $9774-$97C9 compares it with 15 to tell a tap from a hold (a tap fires, a hold does something else) and clears it whenever the button changes.
Written at $9934 and $9AF6 and read once, at $9AC2, inside the raster handler's screen-write helper at $9AC2-$9AEB, where it is the count of bytes still to write. Purely local to that routine.

Counts frames until voice 3 is gated: $9A37 decrements it each frame and $9A3B/$9A44 write $00 or $11 to $D412 accordingly, which is what gives the rotor its pulse. $A7D0 sets the period and $A7CC reads it back.

Low byte of the pointer to the display list being filled this frame. $A9E9/$A9ED set the pair to $0D03 at the start of a sortie and $AA52-$AA61 appends four bytes per shape through it. $BBE6-$BBF4 exchanges it with $9B/$9C once per frame, and $BC05-$BC14 then reads the list back to erase what was drawn last frame.
High byte of the current display-list pointer in $99, set to $0D by $A9ED and exchanged with $9C by $BBEE-$BBF2 once per frame.

Low byte of the pointer to the display list built on the previous frame, $0DA3 at the start of a sortie ($A9F1/$A9F5). $BBE6-$BBF4 exchanges it with $99/$9A every frame so that the list just finished becomes the one $BC05 replays to erase.
High byte of the previous display-list pointer in $9B, set to $0D by $A9F5 and exchanged with $9A at $BBF0-$BBF4.

Number of bytes used in the display list $99/$9A points at, so four times the number of shapes queued. $A9E3 clears it, $AA4E/$AA64 advance it by four per entry, $BC96 compares the replay index with it and $BC9F zeroes it when the replay is finished.

Number of bytes used in the previous frame's display list $9B/$9C. $A9E5 clears it and $BBF8/$BBFC exchanges it with $9D once per frame. Nothing between $9F and $C4 is touched anywhere in $8000-$BFFF.

The KERNAL's 'matrix code of the key currently down' ($40 when none), written by the scan routine $FF9F that the raster handler calls at $9A63. The game reads it in one place only: $98BC-$98D7 watches for code $3F, RUN/STOP, and uses it as a pause key - SID volume to 0, wait for the key to be released, wait for it to be pressed and released again, volume back to $0F. Nothing above $C5 is touched.

The KERNAL's shift-mode flag. The raster handler writes $80 here at $9A5E, which disables the CBM+SHIFT character-set toggle, immediately before calling the keyboard scan at $FF9F that feeds the RUN/STOP pause check at $98BC. It is the only byte of page 2 the game touches.

Low byte of the KERNAL IRQ vector. $A7AE-$A7B0 writes $F2 here (and $99 into $0315) as the last step of starting the game, so every raster interrupt enters the game's handler at $99F2. Written nowhere else; the KERNAL's own handler is never reached again.
High byte of the KERNAL IRQ vector, set to $99 by $A7B3-$A7B5 alongside $0314, giving the raster handler address $99F2.

Low byte of the KERNAL NMI vector, set to $AB by $98DF-$98E1 during start-up so that pressing RESTORE lands in the game's own handler at $9AAB instead of the KERNAL's. $9AAB is a bare rti, so RESTORE does nothing.
High byte of the KERNAL NMI vector, set to $9A by $98E4-$98E6 alongside $0318, giving the NMI address $9AAB.

Low bytes of the bitmap row addresses, 168 entries at $0A00-$0AA7 with the matching high bytes at $0AA8. Entry x is the address of the bitmap row x pixels above the bottom of the screen, so entry 0 is screen pixel row 199 at $3E07 and entry 167 is pixel row 32 at $2500, the first row below the four-row text panel. Built at run time by $BF3B-$BF61, never loaded from the cartridge image. This first 64 bytes covers rows 0-63; the low byte runs 07,06..00 inside a character row and the pattern repeats every 32 entries because four character rows span $500 bytes.

Low bytes of the bitmap row addresses for rows 64-127, the middle third of the table that starts at $0A00. The values repeat the 32-entry cycle 07..00, C7..C0, 87..80, 47..40 because consecutive character rows are 320 ($140) bytes apart, so the low byte advances by $40 per character row.

Low bytes of the bitmap row addresses for rows 128-167, the last 40 entries of the table that starts at $0A00. Entry 167 (at $0AA7) is $00, the first byte of character row 4 of the bitmap; the table ends here and the high bytes begin at $0AA8.

High bytes of the bitmap row addresses, 168 entries at $0AA8-$0B4F matching the low bytes at $0A00. Eight consecutive entries share a value because eight pixel rows live inside one character row; the values run $25,$26,$27,$28,$2A... up to $3E, i.e. the address falls by 320 bytes for each character row nearer the top of the screen. The drawing code eors the byte it reads here with $0F, which adds $40 and so selects the bank-1 bitmap at $6000 instead of the bank-0 one at $2000. This first 64 bytes covers rows 0-63 ($3E down to $34).
High bytes of the bitmap row addresses for rows 64-127, the middle of the table that starts at $0AA8. Values $34 down to $2B, one per character row, eight entries each.

High bytes of the bitmap row addresses for rows 128-167 (the table continues to $0B4F), values $30 down to $25. The cold start also uses this address as the second of the five sta $xx00,y in its clear loop at $BF10, which is what zeroes $0B00-$0BFF.

Last sixteen entries of the bitmap row high-byte table: rows 152-167, high bytes $26 and then $25. $0B4F is the last byte of the table; the individual game variables start immediately afterwards at $0B50.

Flag of the helicopter handler: $ADF4 and $ADFE write it and $AF7A tests it with bit, so only bit 7 matters to the reader. Set on one path through $ADF2-$AE00 and cleared on the other. Meaning not established.

Byte written by $ADA8 inside the helicopter drawer and read back at $ADC9 and $AE1A, where $AE1A adds it to something before the next shape is placed. A local temporary of $AD8F-$AE20; meaning not established.

Height in rows of the rectangle being erased by the display-list replay. $BC5C copies it from $7C (the entry's height, looked up in the table at $94B0) and $BC60-$BC75 trims it where the rectangle would run off the top of the 168-row play area; $BC7C skips the erase when nothing is left, otherwise $BC81 stores it as the second byte of the synthetic shape header at $0E44.

Fire-button state from the previous poll: $FF when the button was up ($97A1, $97CE) and $00 when a press has been taken ($9788, $97BF). $977B and $97B4 test bit 7, so the button only acts on the transition from up to down, and $96A2/$96AB call the two pollers many times a frame without retriggering.

Latch for the left/right stick: $9800 sets it to $FF when a turn starts and $9842 clears it when the stick comes back to centre, so $97F9 and $983B can tell the start and the end of a turn apart. Read nowhere else.

Index 0-15 of the person record being processed by the scan at $9B7D. $9B7F clears it, $9DC9 increments it, and $9DCF stops the scan at 16; $9DD3-$9DD5 shifts it left twice to make the byte offset into the four-byte records at $0CA0.

Saves the record offset of the person being processed across the calls at $9C13-$9C4A and $9D30-$9D45 that pick a random number or draw a shape, both of which use X. Restored with ldx immediately afterwards.

Written at $9E68 and $9E85 and read at $9E7F, $9EDE and $9F09, all inside $9E55-$9F0E, the routine that moves a person between the ground and the helicopter. It holds a record offset; the exact role is not established.
Written once at $9E94 and read at $9EC1 and $9EEF, inside the same routine as $0B57. It holds a second record offset so two person records can be updated together. Meaning not established.
Written at $A141 and $A1C3 and tested with bit at $A20F and $A23B, so only its top bits are read. Local to the actor-movement code at $A10A-$A240; meaning not established.

Written at $A2C6, read at $A2CC as an index and at $A349. It carries an actor slot offset from $A2C6 to the code at $A2CC-$A349 that copies one actor's position into another. The three bytes $0B5B-$0B5D that its span covers are touched by no instruction in $8000-$BFFF.

Frequency low byte of the rotor sound on SID voice 1. $996B-$999B slides it up by $10 a frame towards $C0 while $5D is non-zero and down by $10 a frame towards $30 while it is zero, writing every new value straight to $D400; $A781 presets it when an effect starts. Voice 1 is gated on only while $0CE0 is non-zero.
Written once at $A8B8 and read once at $A921, carrying a value from the helicopter update into the routine at $A91A that adds it to the horizontal speed $5A. Meaning not established.
Counts the three passes of the loop at $AA98-$AABE that tests and draws the three background layers: $AA95 sets it to 3 and $AAB5 decrements it, with $AABA/$AABC stepping the position between passes.
Written at $AC25 and $AC2D and read at $AC1D and $AC30 (as an index), inside the helicopter-shape chooser at $AC14-$AC40. It remembers which of two shape slots was used last. Meaning not established.
The same pattern as $0B61 one routine later: written at $AC85 and $AC8D and read at $AC7D and $AC90 as an index, inside $AC79-$ACA0. Meaning not established.
Written at $B2AA and read at $B2E3, where it is subtracted; it carries a value across the routine at $B2AA-$B2E8 that moves an actor by its velocity fields. Meaning not established.

Saves the actor slot offset ($72) across the routines at $B665 and $B6ED that allocate one or two extra actor records: $B667 and $B6EF store it, $B6E7, $B6FC and $B737 put it back into $72 so the caller's actor is current again when they return.
Second saved slot offset used with $0B64 by $B665: $B6D7 stores the first of the two new records while $B6DC links the second into the actor list, and $B6DF gets it back so it can be linked in too.

Saves an actor's +3 field across the call to $B2AA at $B815: $B80D stores it, $B812 zeroes the field so the move routine leaves it alone, and $B81A/$B81D puts it back. Local to the actor handler at $B73D-$B8AB.

Set to 0 at $B73F and to $FF at $B778 depending on whether the actor's shape was actually drawn this frame; $B7DA tests bit 7 and $B82B tests it for zero, so the actor only moves and only spawns while it is visible.

Saves the slot offset of the actor that is spawning while $B845-$B881 fills in and links the new record, and $B884/$B887 restores it into $72 afterwards. $B84F also uses it as the Y index that copies the parent's position into the child.

Counts the four passes of the loop at $B8D2-$B96D that draws the four numbered objects on the ground: $B8BC clears it, $B960 increments it and $B966 stops at 4. $B8EA and $B92B use it to index the per-object state array at $0CF4.

Low byte of the X position of the first object drawn by $B8D2: $B8C7 derives it from bit 0 of the view origin $75 (so the object lands on an even pixel) with bit 7 set, $B8CA decrements it and $B8D3 reads it back. $B8CF holds the high byte in $0B6B.
High byte of the position whose low byte is $0B6A, set to 3 by $B8CF and incremented by $B96A once per object, which is what spaces the four ground objects 256 pixels apart.

First of the four 16-bit X positions at $0B6C-$0B73 that the hangar drawer $B971 computes and then walks with an index at $BA0B/$BA10. $B9ED writes this low byte; the four positions are drawn with the shape at $8095 and the rows in the table at $BA3B.
High byte of the first hangar position whose low byte is $0B6C, written at $B9F4 and read through the indexed load at $BA10.
Low byte of the second of the four hangar positions, written at $B9D7 after a call to the shift routine $ACF1 has scaled the distance from the view origin. Read only through the index at $BA0B.
High byte of the second hangar position, written at $B9DE and read through the index at $BA10.
Low byte of the third of the four hangar positions, written at $B9C1 from the first scaled distance. Read only through the index at $BA0B.
High byte of the third hangar position, written at $B9C8 and read through the index at $BA10.
Low byte of the fourth hangar position, written at $B9FC as the unscaled distance plus the anchor $78/$79, so this is the nearest of the four and the others are parallax-scaled copies of it.
High byte of the fourth hangar position, written at $BA03. It is the last of the individual variables; the actor record array begins at $0B74.

Actor record array, 10 bytes per slot, indexed by a byte offset in $72 (0, 10, 20 ... 250), so 26 reachable slots at $0B74-$0C77 inside a 30-record grid that ends at $0C9F. Slot 0 is the list header, not an actor: its +8 is the tail link and its +9 the head link, and $B307 starts every pass with ldx $0B7D. This field, +0, is the actor's type, 0-10, which $B30C-$B32E turns into one of the eleven handler addresses in the table at $B32E; $AA01 gives slot 1 type 0, the player's helicopter, and it is never freed.

Field +1 of an actor record: a signed horizontal velocity or step. $B2B3 adds it to the 16-bit world X in +4/+5 once per pass, $A196/$A1A9 and $B7BA/$B7CB walk it up and down within limits (6 and $FA at $B7C0/$B7D1), and $B6C3 and $B729 give a newly spawned actor $18 or $14 with the sign taken from $77.

Field +2 of an actor record: a signed vertical velocity or step. $B2CF adds it to the height field +6, $A251/$A25F and $B7EA/$B7FB step it between fixed bounds, and the collision paths force it to a fixed value ($B5B5 writes 4, $B64C writes 3, $B65F writes 2) to start an actor falling.

Field +3 of an actor record: an animation or sub-state counter. $A22E and $A238 step it, $B77D increments it and wraps it at 3, $A120/$A1B0/$A216 use it as a Y index when picking a shape, and $AEE4/$AF0A/$AF1D eor with it. Note that the free-list initialiser at $AA19 overruns and leaves $0E in this field of slot 1 before the game starts (see $0B7D).

Field +4, the low byte of the actor's 16-bit world X. The whole game works in these coordinates: $A9A9 reads the pair to build a draw position, $B2B0-$B2B6 adds the velocity +1 to it, $B44A and $B578 subtract two actors' X values to measure a distance, and $AEB5/$B093 compare it with the world X in $55/$56.

Field +5, the high byte of the actor's 16-bit world X. Written with +4 everywhere a position is set ($9F49, $A016, $A098, $AFDF, $B031, $B09E, $B695, $B708, $B85B) and used as the high half of every distance calculation ($A14E, $A27D, $B583, $B798).

Field +6, the actor's height in bitmap rows above the row named by +7. $A9C3 adds the two together to get the row the shape is drawn on. $B353 treats a value below $0E as touching the ground and $B380 treats $18 or more as clear of it; $B892-$B8A2 kills an actor whose height leaves the range $0A-$9F, and $B2CC-$B2D2 adds the vertical velocity +2 to it.

Field +7, the bitmap row the actor's height is measured from. Everything standing on the ground gets the ground row $58 (22) here ($AA06, $B6B2, $B716, $B866), and $B349 and $B4BB compare this field with $58 to ask whether an actor is on the ground. $B564 and $B393 subtract two actors' values to see whether they are on the same level.

Field +8, the offset of the previous record in the doubly linked list of live actors. At slot 0 ($0B7C read as an absolute address) it is the list tail. $A937 unlinks a record by writing its predecessor's offset into the successor's +8, and $A95B appends a record by making it the new tail.

Field +9, the offset of the next record in the list, 0 for the end. At slot 0 ($0B7D read as an absolute address) it is the list head, which is how $B307 starts its walk. The same field chains the free pool through $74. $A9F9-$AA0E builds the list with slot 1 (the helicopter) as both head and tail, and $AA11-$AA29 then chains the free slots from offset 20 upward - but the loop runs 27 times instead of 23, so the link stored at offset 250 is 4 rather than 0 and the last four stores land at $0B81, $0B8B, $0B95 and $0B9F, the +3 fields of slots 1 to 4. The free chain therefore has 24 usable records (slots 2 to 25) and would return offset 4, which overlaps slots 0 and 1, if more than 24 actors were ever alive at once. This span also covers slots 1 to 5, $0B7E-$0BAF.

Actor records for slots 6 to 11, $0BB0-$0BEB, ten bytes each with the fields described at $0B74-$0B7D. Slots 2 upward are the free pool at the start of a sortie, chained through their +9 field from $74, and are handed out by $A951 as shots, explosions, hostages and enemy aircraft are created.

Actor records for slots 12 and 13, $0BEC-$0BFF. Nothing distinguishes them from the rest of the pool; the split here is only because the cold start's clear loop makes the disassembler mint a symbol at $0C00.
Actor records for slots 14 to 19, $0C00-$0C3B. This address is also the third of the five sta $xx00,y in the cold start's clear loop at $BF13, which is what zeroes page $0C before the list is built.
Actor records for slots 20 to 25, $0C3C-$0C6D. Slot 25 begins at $0C6E and is the last record the free chain reaches.

Actor record for slot 25, $0C6E-$0C77, the last record a byte index can reach: its offset is 250, so the next would be at 260 and will not fit in the X register. The +9 link here is $04 rather than 0 because of the overrun described at $0B7D. The rest of the 30-record grid, $0C78-$0C9F, is cleared at start-up and never used.

People array, sixteen four-byte records at $0CA0-$0CDF, scanned once per frame by $9B7D with the index in $0B55. This field, +0, is the state: $FF marks a free record ($9B86 skips it, $9BA8, $9DC6, $B640 and $BBC3 set it), otherwise it is a walk phase that $9BDB increments and wraps at 4. $BE52-$BEB1 seeds eight of the sixteen at the start of a sortie with phases 0-3 and X positions spaced about $20-$9E apart from $0750 upward; $BBB5-$BBC6 marks all sixteen free.

Field +1 of a people record: the walking direction. $9BB0-$9BD8 reads it and moves the X position two pixels right for $01, two left for $FF, and leaves it alone for 0. Written at $9C5B, $9C70, $9C77, $9CDA, $9CED, $9D06, $9D12, $9EC9, $9EFE and cleared for every record by $BE7F when the sortie starts.

Field +2, the low byte of a person's 16-bit world X. $9BBE-$9BD3 steps it by two as the person walks, $9BFC, $9C36 and $9CB5 subtract the world X $55/$56 from it to see how far away the helicopter is, and $9DDB uses it to place the shape.

Field +3, the high byte of a person's world X, and the last field of the record. $9B8C-$9B9E compares it with $56 and retires the person (setting +0 to $FF and decrementing $0CF2) when the difference reaches $12 pages, which is how people that scroll off the world are recycled. This span also covers the remaining fifteen records, $0CA4-$0CDF.

Gate for the rotor sound. $9668 sets it to $FF for the playing phase and $95ED, $9635 and $96F1 clear it for the title, the sortie message and the closing screen. $9970 is the only reader: with a zero here $999F silences SID voice 1, otherwise $9975 gates it on and the frequency slide at $997E-$999B runs.

Set at $A0B2 when the actor whose slot offset is kept in $0CE2 is created, and cleared at $AA2E (sortie start), $B63A, $B7B0 and $B8A5 when it dies. $A38C and $B3EC test it before anything uses $0CE2, so it is the 'the slot in $0CE2 is valid' flag. What kind of actor that slot holds is decided outside this range.

The actor slot offset that goes with the flag in $0CE1: $A0B7 stores it when the actor is created, $B3F3 uses it as a Y index and $B630 loads it into $72 so $B2EA can destroy that actor. Meaning beyond 'one particular actor the game keeps a handle on' not established.

Number of entries in the short list of actor slot offsets at $0CE4, 0 to 4. $AA31 clears it at the start of a sortie, $A033-$A03C appends to it, $A39D compares against it, $B386 walks the list backwards from it when a shot is tested against the actors, and $B5F5/$B628 decrement it when an entry is removed.

Up to four actor slot offsets, $0CE4-$0CE7, with the count in $0CE3. $A038 writes an entry, $B38C reads them while testing a falling shot against every listed actor, and $B5FA-$B61B removes one by shifting the later entries down. $B61F destroys the actor an entry names and then removes the entry.
Second entry of the four-slot list that starts at $0CE4: compared at $B5FF and $B604 while an entry is being removed and moved down into $0CE4 by $B60C-$B60F.
Third entry of the four-slot list that starts at $0CE4, moved down into $0CE5 by $B612-$B615 when an earlier entry is removed.

Fourth and last entry of the list that starts at $0CE4, read only at $B618 to fill the gap left in $0CE6. Nothing ever writes it directly, so a full list of four can only be built by $A038 indexing with the count in $0CE3.

Number of entries in the second short list of actor slot offsets, the one at $0CE9; 0 to 4. $AA34 clears it at the start of a sortie, $9F9E-$9FA2 appends to it, $B557 walks it backwards, and $B5C4 and $B5CC decrement it when an entry is removed. The scan at $B55E uses the list to find an actor within ten rows and fourteen pixels of the one being tested.

Up to four actor slot offsets, $0CE9-$0CEC, with the count in $0CE8. $9F77 reads one with a Y index, $B5BC turns an index into a slot offset so $B5C1 can destroy that actor, and $B5D1-$B5F1 removes an entry by shifting the later ones down.
Second entry of the four-slot list that starts at $0CE9: compared at $B5D6, moved down into $0CE9 at $B5E2-$B5E5 and overwritten from $0CEB at $B5E8-$B5EB when an earlier entry goes.
Third entry of the list that starts at $0CE9, compared at $B5DB and moved down into $0CEA at $B5E8-$B5EB.
Fourth and last entry of the list that starts at $0CE9, read only at $B5EE to fill the gap left in $0CEB.

Set to $38 (56) by $BE52 when a sortie's people are seeded, read at $9E31 and decremented at $9EE4. It belongs to the hostage bookkeeping with $0CEE, $0CEF, $0CF0 and $0CF2; 56 plus the 8 records $BE52 seeds on screen is the 64 that $967C and $9687 test for, so it appears to be the reserve of hostages not yet brought into play, but nothing in the code says so outright.

Cleared by the panel reset at $BB8C and incremented at $9E9B. $9679 compares it with $40 (64) and, when all 64 are accounted for here, jumps to $96E8 which prints message 4, MAGNIFICENT!. $9683-$9687 adds $0CEF to it and, when that total reaches 64, prints message 3, THE END, instead.

Cleared by $BB8F and incremented at $9E19 and $B643; $A894-$A897 adds to it in bulk. It is the counterpart of $0CEE in the 64-hostage total tested at $9687: when the two together reach 64 with $0CEE short of 64, the game ends with THE END rather than MAGNIFICENT!.

Set to 8 by $BE52, the number of people seeded on screen at the start of a sortie. $9D20, $9E1C and $B646 decrement it as people leave play and $9EE7 increments it as they arrive; $9E23-$9E36 reads it together with $0CF2 and $0CF1 when the game decides whether to bring another hostage out of the shed.

Cleared by $BB92, incremented at $9D1D and decremented at $9E9E, and read at $9C2B, $9CD1, $9CFD, $9E40, $A885, $A891 and $A89C. $A885-$A89C moves its value into $0CEF in one go, so it counts hostages that are in the helicopter and are lost if it is destroyed. The exact transitions are decided outside this range.

Cleared by $BB95, decremented at $9BA5 and $9C88 and incremented at $9EA1, and read once at $9E23. It counts people records that are alive but off the visible part of the world; $9BA5 decrements it at the same moment $9BAA retires a person that has scrolled $12 pages away.

Number of the player's shots currently alive, 0 to 5. $BED6 clears it at the start of a sortie, $B00C increments it when a shot is created, and $B1DB, $B1E4, $B375, $B3E6 and $B42C decrement it when one hits something or reaches the ground. $97DE-$97E3 refuses to fire when it has reached 5, which is the on-screen limit.

Four bytes, $0CF4-$0CF7, one per numbered object on the ground, all cleared by $BBAA at the start of a sortie. $B65A sets an entry to 1 when its object is hit, $B653 tests it so an object is only hit once, and $B8ED/$B92E read it while $B8D2-$B96D draws the four objects, choosing a damaged shape and adding the extra piece at $809D when the entry is non-zero. $0CF7 is separately set to 1 by $BE63.

Fourth byte of the four-entry ground-object hit array that starts at $0CF4. Cleared with the other three by $BBAA at the start of a sortie and then set to 1 on its own by $BE63 when the sortie's people are seeded, so the fourth object starts the sortie already marked.

Four bytes, $0CF8-$0CFB, one per ground object, all set to $10 (16) by $BBAF at the start of a sortie. $9E5A and $9E70 read an entry and $9EE1 decrements one; sixteen per object times four objects is the 64 hostages the game counts towards in $0CEE. $0CFB is separately set to 8 by $BE5E.

Fourth byte of the four-entry ground-object count array that starts at $0CF8. $BBAF gives all four the value $10 (16) at the start of a sortie and $BE5E then overwrites this one with 8, so the fourth object holds half as many as the other three.

Cleared by the panel reset at $BB9D, read at $A6EE and $B0D8 and rewritten at $A6F3 and $B0DD, both of which are read-modify-write pairs in the routines that place a sound or a shot. Meaning not established.
Cleared by $BBA0 and read and rewritten by the pair at $A3F2/$A3F7 only. A single-routine counter in the enemy-aircraft code; meaning not established.
Cleared by $BBA3 and by $A6D8, and read and rewritten by the pairs at $A3C0/$A3C5 and $A3D9/$A3DE. Like $0CFD it is confined to $A3B0-$A6E0; meaning not established.

Which sortie is being played, 0, 1 or 2. $BB9A clears it when the panel is reset, $964B increments it after each sortie message has been shown, and $961E-$9623 uses it both as the index into the five-message table at $8AD7 (0 FIRST SORTIE, 1 SECOND SORTIE, 2 THIRD SORTIE) and as the test that ends the game: when it reaches 3, $9625 jumps to $96E4 which prints message 3, THE END.

Cleared by $BF02 at the start of a sortie and by the cold start's clear loop at $BF16 (which is what zeroes page $0D). $9D28 sets it, $9EB1 rewrites it and $9EAA tests bit 7, all inside the code that moves a person between the ground and the helicopter. Meaning not established.
Cleared at the top of every frame by $9673 and set at $9D4A; $9D2B tests bit 7. A one-frame flag raised by the people scan and read by the same scan later in the frame. Meaning not established.
Cleared at the top of every frame by $9676 and set at $B0FE; $B0E6 tests bit 7. A one-frame flag raised in the shot-handling code at $B0D2-$B101. Meaning not established.

First of the two display lists, $0D03-$0DA2, 160 bytes holding up to forty four-byte entries: kind, view-relative X low, X high, bitmap row. $A9E9 points $99/$9A here at the start of a sortie and $AA38 appends an entry for every shape the frame draws. $BBE6 swaps the two list pointers each frame so that the list just built becomes the one $BC05 replays to erase. This first 64 bytes holds entries 0-15.

Entries 16 to 31 of the display list that starts at $0D03. Each entry is four bytes and the count of bytes in use is kept in $9D (or $9E once the lists have been swapped), so the list is only ever read as far as it was filled.

Entries 32 to 39, the last eight of the display list that starts at $0D03. Nothing checks for overflow: $AA38 adds four to $9D without a limit, so a frame that queued more than forty shapes would run on into the second list at $0DA3.

Second of the two display lists, $0DA3-$0E42, the same 160-byte, forty-entry layout as $0D03. $A9F1 points $9B/$9C here at the start of a sortie and $BBE6-$BBF4 exchanges the pair with $99/$9A once per frame, so the two lists alternate between 'being built' and 'being replayed to erase'. This first 64 bytes holds entries 0-15.
Entries 16 to 30 of the display list that starts at $0DA3. $BC05-$BC18 walks the list four bytes at a time, rebuilding $71, $6A, $6B and $6C from each entry before erasing the rectangle it describes.

Entries 23 to 38 of the display list that starts at $0DA3. This address is also the fifth destination in the cold start's clear loop, where $BF19, $BF1C and $BF1F are three identical sta $0E00,y instructions: page $0E is zeroed three times over and no other page is cleared by those three stores.

Last entry of the display list that starts at $0DA3: bytes $0E40-$0E42 are the X high byte and row of entry 39, and $0E43 is the one byte of the page that belongs to neither list nor to the scratch word at $0E44.

A two-byte synthetic shape header, width then height, used to erase one display-list entry. $BC84-$BC86 puts the (clipped) width from $7B here and $BC81 the clipped height from $0B52, then $BC89 passes the address $0E44 to $8BBA so the drawing code treats the pair as a shape header, $BC8E loads the position from $6A, and $BC93 calls the solid-rectangle drawer $8C5E. The cold start at $BF26 leaves $FF here.

Height half of the two-byte erase header at $0E44, written by $BC81 from $0B52 and set to $FF by the cold start at $BF29. The bytes above it, $0E46 to $0EFF, are zeroed by $BF06 and read by nothing in $8000-$BFFF.

The blitter's shift-by-0 table: entry y = y, an identity map. $8DF3 selects it by setting zpa_43 to $10 when zpa_09 is 0, i.e. when the shape's screen bit column is a multiple of 8 and the row can be copied straight into the bitmap cells with no shifting at all. Its twin at $1800 is all zeroes for the same reason. This is also why the 4 KB lives here: in VIC bank 0 the VIC sees character ROM at $1000-$1FFF, so the RAM underneath is invisible to the video chip and free for the CPU. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-1: entry y = y >> 1. Read through ($42) by $8FD3 as the part of a shape byte that stays in the current bitmap cell when the shape sits 1 bit right of a cell boundary (zpa_09 = 1, so zpa_43 = $11). Values run 0 to $7F with each result repeated for two consecutive indices, and bit 7 is always clear. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-2: entry y = y >> 2, values 0 to $3F with each repeated four times. Selected when zpa_09 = 2 (zpa_43 = $12), which for a multicolour bitmap is a whole pixel's offset: the commonest case for an object that moves by pixels rather than by cells. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-3: entry y = y >> 3, values 0 to $1F, eight indices per result. Selected when zpa_09 = 3 (zpa_43 = $13). With the twin at $1B00 it lets $8FD3 drop a shape row 3 bits right of a cell boundary with two table reads and an ora per byte. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-4: entry y = y >> 4, so the table is simply the high nibble of its index, $00 repeated sixteen times, then $01 sixteen times, and so on to $0F. Selected when zpa_09 = 4 (zpa_43 = $14), a half-cell offset. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-5: entry y = y >> 5, only eight distinct results 0 to 7, each covering 32 indices. Selected when zpa_09 = 5 (zpa_43 = $15). At this shift most of each source byte has moved on into the next cell, so the companion table at $1D00 carries five of its eight bits. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-6: entry y = y >> 6, four results 0 to 3, each covering 64 indices - it is just the top two bits of the index. Selected when zpa_09 = 6 (zpa_43 = $16). Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Shift-by-7: entry y = y >> 7, so the whole table is $00 for indices $00-$7F and $01 for $80-$FF - the sign bit of the index and nothing else. Selected when zpa_09 = 7 (zpa_43 = $17), the largest sub-cell offset, where all but one bit of every source byte spills into the next cell via $1F00. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

The overflow half for shift 0: every one of its 256 entries is $00. When a shape sits exactly on a cell boundary nothing spills into the next cell, so $8FD3's running overflow zpa_41 stays zero and the ora that merges it is a no-op. Reached through ($44) with zpa_45 = $18, set by $8DF3 from zpa_09. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 1: entry y = (y << 7) and $FF, so $00 when bit 0 of the index is clear and $80 when it is set - the single bit that a 1-bit shift pushes out of the byte. $8FD3 keeps it in zpa_41 and ors it into the next cell to the right; $8E7F also reads this half to seed zpa_41 from the byte clipped off the left of the shape. Selected by zpa_45 = $19. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 2: entry y = (y << 6) and $FF, the index's low two bits lifted to the top, so the table cycles $00, $40, $80, $C0 through all 256 entries. Selected by zpa_45 = $1A. In multicolour terms it carries exactly one pixel into the neighbouring cell. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 3: entry y = (y << 5) and $FF, the index's low three bits raised to bits 7-5, stepping $00, $20, $40 ... $E0 and repeating every eight entries. Selected by zpa_45 = $1B. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 4: entry y = (y << 4) and $FF, i.e. the low nibble of the index moved into the high nibble, so the table counts $00, $10, $20 ... $F0 and repeats every sixteen entries. Selected by zpa_45 = $1C. Half of every source byte crosses the cell boundary at this shift. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 5: entry y = (y << 3) and $FF, the low five bits of the index raised to bits 7-3, so the values step by 8 and repeat every 32 entries. Selected by zpa_45 = $1D. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 6: entry y = (y << 2) and $FF, the low six bits of the index raised by two places, stepping by 4 and repeating every 64 entries. Selected by zpa_45 = $1E. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Overflow half for shift 7: entry y = (y << 1) and $FF, the index doubled with bit 7 dropped, so every value is even and only the index's top bit fails to cross into the next cell. Selected by zpa_45 = $1F, the largest sub-cell offset the blitter uses. Built at run time by $BF63-$BF98, which walks the shift count 0-7 in $008E, points $6F/$70 at $1000+256*n and $8F/$90 at $1800+256*n, and for every y runs n rounds of lsr a / ror zpa_6D so the byte that stays and the byte that spills fall out of the same shift.

Character set, 2 KB at $5000-$57FF, eight bytes per glyph. It is a byte-for-byte copy of the LOWER half of the C64 character ROM, $D000-$D7FF, the upper-case and graphics set; the copy is made once at start-up by $BFA8-$BFC9, which clears bit 2 of $01 to bring the ROM into view at $D000 first. The VIC only reads it in bank 1: the raster handler puts $04 in bits 3-1 of $D018 for the text rows, giving a character base of bank + $1000, which is $5000 in bank 1 and the ROM itself in bank 0. This first block is glyphs $00-$07: @ A B C D E F G. Letters are used by the five centred messages ($8AE1 FIRST SORTIE onward) and the title screen strings at $9B0D.

Glyphs $08-$0F of the character set: H I J K L M N O. H, I, L, M, N and O all appear in the title strings CHOPLIFTER!, DAN GORLIN, DANE BIGHAM and in the messages MAGNIFICENT! and THE END that $8A8B prints into the mid-screen text window.
Glyphs $10-$17 of the character set: P Q R S T U V W. P, R, S and T carry the words PRESENTS, FIRST SORTIE, SECOND SORTIE and THIRD SORTIE; the game never displays Q, V or W.

Glyphs $18-$1F: X Y Z, then the four symbols that end the first quarter of the set - left bracket, pound sign, right bracket, up arrow - and the left arrow at $1F. None of these seven are used by the game; only X, Y and Z could appear, and no string contains them.

Glyphs $20-$27: space, exclamation mark, double quote, hash, dollar, percent, ampersand, apostrophe. The space at $20 is what $98EB and $9AB2 fill the text rows with, and the exclamation mark at $21 ends CHOPLIFTER! and MAGNIFICENT!. Screen code $26 also appears in the video matrix below the text panel, but there it is a pair of colour nibbles for the multicolour bitmap, not a glyph.

Glyphs $28-$2F: open and close parentheses, asterisk, plus, comma, minus, full stop, slash. The parentheses are used by the title line (C) 1982 at $9B4D. Screen code $2E, the full stop, fills the whole of the video matrix below the text panel, but as the colour pair red/light blue for the multicolour bitmap rather than as a glyph.

Glyphs $30-$37: the digits 0 to 7. The three two-digit counters in the status panel are drawn straight out of this block - $A982 adds $30 to a nibble and $A985 stores the result into the video matrix at $0450,y and $4450,y - and the year in (C) 1982 uses 1, 8, 9 and 2.

Glyphs $38-$3F: the digits 8 and 9, then colon, semicolon, less-than, equals, greater-than and question mark. Only 8 and 9 are ever displayed; they complete the digit run the status-panel counters draw from.

Glyphs $40-$47, the first of the box-drawing blocks. $40 and $43 are a horizontal rule on scanlines 3-4, $44 one scanline higher (2-3), $45 higher again (1-2) and $46 one lower (4-5); $42 is a vertical rule on columns 3-4 and $47 one on columns 2-3. $41 is the spade. The status panel uses $44 for the top edge of its frame, $46 for the bottom edge, and $41 as the icon in front of the first counter, written by $BB2F to $0458 and $4458.

Glyphs $48-$4F: a vertical rule on columns 4-5 ($48), the rounded corners for the top right ($49), bottom left ($4A) and bottom right ($4B) of a box, the square bottom-left corner ($4C), the two diagonals ($4D falling, $4E rising) and the square top-left corner ($4F). The status panel draws $49 at the right end of its top rule and $4A and $4B at the two ends of its bottom rule.

Glyphs $50-$57: the square top-right corner ($50), a filled disc ($51), a thick bar on scanlines 5-6 ($52), the heart ($53), a vertical rule on columns 1-2 ($54), the rounded top-left corner ($55), a diagonal cross ($56) and a hollow circle ($57). The status panel uses $54 for the left side of its frame, $55 for the top-left corner, and $53 as the icon of the third counter, written by $BB3F to $046E and $446E.

Glyphs $58-$5F: the club ($58), a vertical rule on columns 5-6 ($59), the diamond ($5A), a full cross ($5B), a staggered vertical dashed line ($5C), a centred vertical rule ($5D), the pi sign ($5E) and a filled corner triangle ($5F). The panel uses $59 for the right side of its frame and $5A as the icon of the second counter, written by $BB37 to $0463 and $4463.

Glyphs $60-$67: a blank cell ($60), the left half block ($61), the lower half block ($62), a rule along the very top scanline ($63) and along the very bottom ($64), the left quarter block of two columns ($65), a fine checkerboard ($66) and the right quarter block of two columns ($67). $65 and $67 are the two glyphs the status panel uses in reverse video ($E5 and $E7) to cap the ends of its red bars.

Glyphs $68-$6F: a checkerboard confined to the lower half ($68), a filled triangle in the upper-left corner ($69), the right quarter block ($6A), a left-hand tee ($6B), the lower-right quarter block ($6C) and three more tee and corner pieces ($6D, $6E) ending with a rule two scanlines deep along the bottom ($6F). The game displays none of them.

Glyphs $70-$77: a corner piece ($70), an upward tee ($71), a downward tee ($72), a right-hand tee ($73), the two-column left block ($74), the three-column left block ($75), the three-column right block ($76) and a rule two scanlines deep along the top ($77). The game displays none of them.

Glyphs $78-$7F, the last of the normal half: three-scanline rules top and bottom ($78, $79), the two-column right block ($7A) and five quarter-block and half-block shapes ($7B-$7F). The game displays none of them; $7F is the last glyph before the reversed copy of the whole set begins at $5400.

Reversed half of the character set, $5400-$57FF, glyphs $80-$FF: every byte here is the ones complement of the byte 2 KB earlier, which is how the C64 ROM stores its reverse-video images. This block is $80-$87, the reversed @ A B C D E F G. Setting bit 7 of a screen code selects these, and the game only ever uses three of them, all in the status panel.
Glyphs $88-$8F: the reversed H I J K L M N O. Nothing in the game writes a screen code in this range; the messages and title strings are all printed in normal video.
Glyphs $90-$97: the reversed P Q R S T U V W, unused by the game.
Glyphs $98-$9F: the reversed X Y Z, brackets, pound sign, up arrow and left arrow. Unused.

Glyphs $A0-$A7: the reversed space, exclamation mark, double quote, hash, dollar, percent, ampersand and apostrophe. $A0, the reversed space, is a solid block and is the single most visible glyph in the game: $9B6C-$9B71 fills $0451-$0476 in both video matrices with it and colours those cells red, which is what draws the three long bars of the status panel.
Glyphs $A8-$AF: the reversed parentheses, asterisk, plus, comma, minus, full stop and slash. Unused by the game; the panel bars use $A0 from the previous block.
Glyphs $B0-$B7: the reversed digits 0 to 7. The status-panel counters are drawn in normal video from $5180, so these are never displayed.
