Otherwise files it in the frame's object list as kind 2 via $AA38 and plots it, mirrored or not according to bit 2 of the actor's world-X low byte, which animates the tracks as the tank rolls. Then sets up the turret at offset (-$07, +3) with $A9A0.
Inline argument of the $8BF9 at $A0F3: the pointer $0067, holding the turret's draw position, the tank's world X less 7 and its Y plus 3, as just computed by $A9A0.
The jsr $8BE0 that loads the turret's bitmap address from the inline pointer below.

Inline argument of the $8BE0 at $A0F8: the pointer $8057, entry 39 of the shape pointer table at $8009. Shape 39 is 15 bitmap bits by 3 rows, the small block that sits on the hull and carries the gun.

Clips and plots the turret, filing it in the frame's object list as kind 3 through $AA38; unlike the hull it is never mirrored. Then picks the barrel: the aim index $0B77 (0 to 4) doubled indexes the shape pointer table at entry 41, so entries 41 to 45 are the gun at five elevations, and the address goes into $65/$66 for the $8BE0 that follows.

Inline argument of the $8BE0 at $A11B: the pointer $0065, where the code has just put the address of shape-table entry 41 + the aim index, the gun barrel at the elevation the tank is currently holding.

Positions the gun barrel. The aim index $0B77 indexes $A244 for the horizontal offset ($0B, $07, $01, $FF, $FB, i.e. the muzzle swings from eleven units left of the tank's origin to five units right as the gun comes up) and the vertical offset is a fixed +7, above the turret. $A9A0 turns that into a draw position in $67/$68/$69.
Inline argument of the $8BF9 at $A12D: the pointer $0067, the gun barrel's draw position as just computed by $A9A0.

Clips and plots the gun barrel, filing it as kind 4 in the frame's object list, and then runs the whole of the tank's thinking. $81/$82 becomes the helicopter's world X minus the tank's and $83 the difference in height. A tank more than three pages away is destroyed on the spot ($B5CC then $A937). Inside $80 units the fire timer $0B75 counts down and, at zero, is reloaded with 8 plus a random 0..15 and the aim re-decided: if the helicopter's bearing already falls inside the window the current aim index covers ($A249 and $A24A) the shot flag $0B59 is set and $A2C4 fires. Otherwise the tank drives - toward the helicopter normally, away from it while the wreck burns ($61) - and nudges the aim index one notch toward the right window.

Five signed bytes, $0B $07 $01 $FF $FB, indexed by a tank's aim index $0B77 at $A123. They are subtracted from the tank's world X by $A9A0 to place the gun barrel, so the muzzle sits eleven units left of the tank's origin at the lowest elevation and five units right at the highest.

The low end of the bearing window for aim index 0: a single byte $00. Read at $A1B5 and $A21B alongside $A24A; because the two tables overlap by four bytes, index n's window is $A249+n to $A24A+n, i.e. $00-$40, $40-$70, $70-$90, $90-$C0, $C0-$FF.

Five bytes, $40 $70 $90 $C0 $FF: the high end of the bearing window for each of the tank's five aim indices, and, offset by one, the low ends for indices 1 to 4. The bearing compared against them is $81, the helicopter's world X minus the tank's, biased by $80 so that $80 means level. The tank fires when the helicopter lies inside the window its gun is already pointing at ($A1B5), and otherwise steps the aim index one notch toward the window it does lie in ($A21B). The windows are unequal so the gun lingers on the middle elevations.

Keeps a tank rolling the way it was already going, used while its fire timer has not expired. Reads the drift $0B76: zero means it was standing still, so it stays still ($A25B); positive means it was moving right ($A271); negative means left ($A2AB).
Stops a tank where it is by clearing its drift byte $0B76. Called when the tank decides to sit and shoot rather than close on the helicopter.

Drives a tank away from the helicopter: if the bearing $81 says the helicopter is to the right ($81 negative, i.e. past $80) it goes right, otherwise left. Used when the helicopter is wrecked and when a random draw at $A1E2 or $A1F9 tells the tank to back off.

Drives a tank toward the helicopter: the mirror of $A263, going right when the bearing $81 says the helicopter is to the right. This is the normal approach behaviour and also what $A1CC uses when the machine has been destroyed.

Moves a tank four world units to the right and records the direction by setting its drift $0B76 to +4. It first refuses to cross the right-hand end of the battlefield: with $6D = $1174 minus the tank's world X, the move is abandoned when $6D has fallen to $C0 minus eight times the tank's rank $0B7B, minus one, and abandoned outright once the tank is already past $1174. Rank is 5 to 12 and unique among live tanks ($9F69), so tanks halt between about 95 and 151 units short of $1174 and each stops at its own distance instead of piling onto the same spot.

Moves a tank four world units to the left, sixteen-bit, and records the direction by setting its drift $0B76 to $FC (-4). There is no limit on this side: a tank that keeps going left eventually passes three pages from the helicopter and is deleted by the range check at $A16B.

Fires a tank shell. Called from $A241 when the aim check has set $0B59. Saves the tank's own slot in $0B5A, takes a fresh slot with $A951 and builds an actor of type 8 (handler $B26D, outside this range) in it: world X = the tank's minus $10, then shifted again by $A34F indexed on the aim index plus the tank's own drift, so a shell from a moving tank inherits its speed and a steeper gun throws the muzzle further forward; height $0B7A = the tank's plus 9 and rank $0B7B = the tank's plus 1, which puts the shell at the muzzle rather than the hull. The velocity comes from three more tables indexed by the same aim index: $A354 gives $0B75 the vertical component $F4, $F9, $00, $07, $0C (-12 to +12) with the tank's drift added, $A359 gives $0B76 a constant 3 and $A35E gives $0B77 the value 2, 3, 4, 3 or 2. $A95B links the shell into the display list and $72 is restored to the tank's own slot before returning, so the handler can carry on.

Five bytes, $00 $06 $10 $19 $1F, indexed at $A2EA by the firing tank's aim index. Added to the shell's starting world X (already the tank's minus $10), with the tank's own drift on top, so the shell leaves the muzzle rather than the middle of the hull and the offset grows as the gun comes up.

Five signed bytes, $F4 $F9 $00 $07 $0C (-12, -7, 0, +7, +12), indexed at $A332 by the firing tank's aim index. The tank's own drift $0B76 is added and the sum becomes the new shell's $0B75, its vertical velocity component. The five values are the elevations that go with shapes 41 to 45.

Five bytes, all $03, indexed at $A33A by the firing tank's aim index and stored into the shell's $0B76. Every shell leaves at the same horizontal speed of 3 whatever the elevation; the table exists so the launch code can be written once, and the five entries could be given different values without touching the code.

Five bytes, $02 $03 $04 $03 $02, indexed at $A340 by the firing tank's aim index and stored into the shell's $0B77. Symmetrical about the level gun, so the shell's own handler at $B26D draws or steers a steeply climbing and a steeply falling shell the same way.

The game's spawn clock, called once per tick from $96CC (118 hits in 118 ticks, live). Two gates on the tick counter $89. Every fourth tick it calls $9E22, which is what puts hostages out of the barracks and takes them out of the helicopter at the base. Then it returns immediately unless $89 AND $2F is zero, which is true for eight of every 256 ticks, and that slower beat drives the vehicles: a random byte from $DC04 and the difficulty level $8D decide between three outcomes. At $8D >= 2, with the spare bits of the random byte clear and $0CE1 showing no type-10 actor alive, $A044 makes one. Otherwise, if the random byte is positive and the type-9 count $0CE3 has not reached the limit in $A3B6, $9FA6 makes a type-9. Failing both, if the live tank count $0CE8 is below the limit in $A3B2, $9F12 makes a tank. At $8D = 0 only tanks can appear.

Four bytes, $01 $02 $01 $01, indexed by the difficulty level $8D at $A3AA and compared against $0CE8, the number of tanks currently alive. One tank at a time at difficulty 0, two at 1, and back to one at 2 and 3 - where the aircraft spawned by $9FA6 and $A044 take over the pressure.

Four bytes, $00 $01 $02 $02, indexed by the difficulty level $8D at $A39A and compared against $0CE3, the number of type-9 actors alive. The comparison is an equality test, so the limit is also the count: none at all at difficulty 0, one at 1, two at 2 and 3.

Adds one, in BCD, to $0CFE, the number of hostages aboard the helicopter shown in the middle field of the status bar, and redraws it by calling $A978 with X = 1, which writes the two digits at screen offsets $0464 and $0465, just after the diamond glyph, in both text matrices. Saves and restores X and Y. Called from $9D18 when a hostage climbs in.

Subtracts one, in BCD, from $0CFE and redraws the middle status-bar field through $A978 with X = 1, the counterpart of $A3BA. Saves and restores X and Y. Called from $9EA4 when a hostage is put down at the home base.

Adds one, in BCD, to $0CFD, the tally of hostages safely delivered, and redraws the right-hand status-bar field by calling $A978 with X = 2, which writes the two digits at screen offsets $046F and $0470, just after the heart glyph. Then plays the two-note rising cue through $A7C7 with voice parameters ($2B, 1) and ($40, 2) before restoring X and Y. Called from $9EA7, once per hostage set down at the base. The third, leftmost field of the bar is the casualty counter $0CFC, which $B0D2 owns.

Tail of the routine that starts at $A3EC. That routine adds 1 in binary-coded decimal to $0CFD and redraws it as the third (heart) status-bar counter; here it plays two effects through $A7C7 - pitch $2B held one frame, then pitch $40 held two - and restores the caller's X and Y from $84/$85. Its only caller, $9EA7, runs immediately after $9EA4 has called $A3D3 to take one off the second (diamond) counter $0CFE, so the pair moves one unit from the second counter to the third.

Turns this frame's joystick reading into the helicopter's two velocities; called first thing every frame from $A4C7. The horizontal velocity $51/$52 (signed 16-bit, world units times 256) is dragged by one sixteenth of itself, then the thrust word from $A4AB/$A4AC indexed by 2*|$5B| is subtracted when the stick is left ($5B = +5) and added when it is right ($5B = -5); the result is clamped to exactly +/-$1500 with the low byte zeroed. The vertical velocity $53/$54 is then moved toward the target climb rate $A4B7[$5C]: the gap is halved while it is 2 or more, up to twice, so it closes by a quarter of the distance a frame. $53 is always cleared, so only the high byte of the vertical velocity survives.
clamp the horizontal velocity to exactly +/-$1500, low byte zeroed

Low bytes of six 16-bit horizontal thrust values, one per stick deflection 0..5: $0000, $0060, $00B4, $0108, $015C, $01A4. $A413 adds or subtracts entry |$5B| to the helicopter's velocity. Only entry 5 ($01A4 = 420 units per frame) is ever used, because $A741 only ever puts 0 or +/-5 in $5B.
High bytes of the same six thrust values; $A413 reads $A4AB,y and $A4AC,y with y = 2*|$5B| as one little-endian word, so the pair at index 5 is $01A4.

Target vertical velocity (the high byte of $53/$54) indexed by $5C, sixteen signed bytes $F6,$F7..$FF,$00,$01..$04,$06 - that is index minus 10, except index 15 which is +6 rather than +5. Only five indices occur: 0 (both up and down pressed) gives -10, 2 (forced by $A738 once the helicopter has been hit) -8, 5 (stick down, or stick centred in flight) -5, $0A (stick centred on the ground) 0, and $0F (stick up) +6. Read by $A413.

One frame of helicopter flight, called from the type-0 actor handler at $B0CE. $A413 turns the stick into the velocities $51/$52 and $53/$54, then one of two models runs: $A615 while $5D says the machine is airborne, $A4DA while it is in contact with the ground. Finishes by tail-calling $A7D6, which re-decides airborne-or-grounded for next frame and handles the base window, the stopped flag and the hit sequence. Verified live: with the helicopter parked only $A4DA is hit, and holding up switches every hit to $A615.

The ground-contact flight model, used while $5D is clear. If a hard contact was flagged last frame ($60) it is cleared, the altitude $57 is nudged back up by one and $A5BE bounces the vertical velocity. Otherwise, with the helicopter level ($5A = 0): a descent faster than about -5.4 units a frame sets $60, drops $57 by one and adds the ground push of $A5E1 - the hard landing; a gentler descent simply bounces; anything not descending gets the ground push. Every path except a banked skid halves $51/$52, which is the skid friction. If the vertical velocity has turned positive the machine has lifted off and control passes straight to $A615; otherwise the new bank angle is worked out at $A556 as $5A minus (($51/$52 plus or minus $53/$54) shifted right 9), never allowed past level and clamped to +/-5, and handed to $A8B8.
hard-contact recovery: altitude back up one
hard contact: flag it, drop the altitude one and add the ground push

Bounces the helicopter off the ground: shifts the vertical velocity $53/$54 right by 3 + $61 places and negates it, so a normal touchdown keeps an eighth of the impact speed and one after the machine has been hit ($61 set) only a sixteenth. This is what makes the helicopter rock on its skids after a landing.

Adds the ground's upward push to the vertical velocity $53/$54. The base impulse is the constant $04B0 held at $A613/$A614; while the helicopter is already rising it is shifted right by (($53/$54)*8 >> 8) places, so the push fades out the faster the machine climbs, and while it is descending the full value is used. This is the spring that lifts the helicopter off the ground and then holds it just above it.
Low byte of the constant $04B0 (1200), the base upward impulse $A5E1 loads into $7F/$80 as the helicopter's ground push.
High byte of that same constant $04B0; $A5E1 reads $A613 and $A614 as a little-endian pair.

The airborne flight model, used while $5D is set. Steps the bank angle $5A one unit toward the stick position $5B and shifts the world X by one unit in the same direction as it does so. Then adds ($51/$52) shifted right 8 to the world X $55/$56 and clamps it to the playfield - $02D0 at the left edge, $12D0 at the right - zeroing the horizontal velocity at either limit. Finally adds ($53/$54) shifted right 8 to the altitude $57, clamped to 0 below and $70 above, and zeroes the vertical velocity when $57 reaches $70; that is the ceiling, confirmed live by holding up until $57 sticks at $70 with $53/$54 at zero.
ceiling: altitude pinned at $70 and the vertical velocity killed

Zeroes $0CFE, the second (diamond) status-bar counter, and redraws it through $A978 with X = 1; preserves the caller's X and Y in $84/$85. Called from $A88D at the end of the helicopter's settle sequence. $0CFE is the counter $A3BA increments and $A3D3 decrements one at a time.

Adds A, in binary-coded decimal, to $0CFC - the first (spade) status-bar counter - redraws it through $A978 with X = 0, and then plays a four-note rising figure on the effects channel: pitches $18, $2C, $39 and $5B, each held two frames by $A7C7, which busy-waits so they come out as a melody rather than one note. Returns without doing anything at all when A is zero. Preserves the caller's X and Y in $84/$85. Called from exactly one place, $A888, with the value of $0CF1.

Reads the up and down bits of joystick port 1 and leaves a climb-rate index in $5C; called once a frame from $969C. $DC01 masked to two bits gives 3 centred, 2 up, 1 down, 0 both (the lines are active low), and $A73D maps those to $0A, $0F, $05 and $00. Centred while the helicopter is on the ground ($5D clear) is rewritten as 'down', which is how a parked machine is held against the ground. If the helicopter has been hit ($61 or $63 non-zero) the index is overridden with 2, and $A4B7 turns that into a forced descent of -8.

The four climb-rate indices $A71A can store in $5C, selected by the low two bits of $DC01: $00 when up and down are pressed together, $05 for down alone, $0F for up alone, $0A for centred. $A4B7 turns the index into a target vertical velocity.

Reads the left and right bits of joystick port 1 ($DC01 shifted right twice and masked) and stores the bank command in $5B through the table at $A758: +5 for left, -5 for right, 0 for centred or both. Forced to 0 once $63 is set, so the player loses lateral control after the helicopter is finished. Called once a frame from $969F. $5B is the target bank angle - $A615 steps $5A toward it and $A413 turns it into horizontal thrust.
The four values $A741 can put in $5B, indexed by the left/right bits of $DC01: $00 both pressed, $FB (-5) right, $05 (+5) left, $00 centred.

Sets the SID up for the engine and installs the raster interrupt; called once from $95A2 before play begins. SID: master volume 15, filter off ($D418 = $0F, and $D417 is never written). Voice 2 gets the frequency register $041A, which sets how fast its noise generator is clocked, and a percussive envelope of attack 4, decay 2, sustain 1, release 0 ($D407, $D408, $D40C, $D40D); the raster handler re-gates it at $9A50 whenever the counter $95 runs out, reloading $95 from $94, which is started here at $11 - so voice 2 is the rotor chop and $94 is its period in frames. Voice 1 gets frequency high byte $01 and sustain 3, release 0 ($D401, $D406); its low byte is the sliding value $0B5E, started here at $30, which $996B walks between $30 and $C0 in steps of $10 - upward while the helicopter is airborne, which also shortens $94 so the chop quickens, and back down on the ground - so voice 1 is a noise rumble sweeping $0130 to $01C0 and $94 falls from $11 toward 8 as the machine climbs (read back live at the ceiling: $0B5E = $C0, $94 = $08). Voice 3 gets sustain 15, release 0 ($D414) and is then left for the sound effects $A7C7 fires. No waveform or gate register is written here: $9977 gates voice 1 with $81 and $9A57 re-gates voice 2 with $81, both of which select noise, while $9A44 gates voice 3 with $11, which selects triangle. Interrupts: both CIA interrupt masks are cleared ($7F to $DC0D and $DD0D, then both registers read to drop anything pending), the VIC raster interrupt is enabled ($01 to $D01A), the raster high bit in $D011 is cleared, the first compare line is set to $1E, $0314/$0315 are pointed at the handler $99F2 and interrupts are let in with cli.

Decides whether a sound may be started: returns carry clear (go ahead) only when bit 7 of $8C is set - the flag $95AD sets when play starts and $96F4 clears - and the helicopter's settle counter $62 is not exactly 6. Carry set means stay silent. Used by $A7C7 before every effect and by the engine-sound update $996B.

Starts one sound effect on SID voice 3, which the raster handler gates with $11, a triangle. X is the frequency high byte, written straight to $D40F ($D40E is never written, so the low byte stays 0); Y is the length in frames, latched in $98, which $9A37 counts down before gating the voice off. If an effect is still sounding the routine loops here until $98 reaches zero, so consecutive calls come out as a tune instead of overwriting each other. Returns at once without touching the SID when $A7BA says sound is off. Callers pass the pitch in X: $3A for the gun ($97ED), $2B then $40 for a death ($A400), $18/$2C/$39/$5B for the four-note figure at $A6FF, $78 from the tank code at $B88D.

Runs after the flight model each frame and settles everything that depends on where the helicopter ended up; reached as a tail call from $A4D7. First it compares the altitude $57 with the minimum ground clearance for the current bank angle - $9471 indexed by 2*(signed bank + 5), values 7 to 10, the same table $A8B8 uses as the shape's vertical anchor. Above that the machine is airborne: $5D is set, the 'stopped' and 'over the base' flags $5E and $5F are cleared and the routine returns. At or below it the altitude is clamped up to the minimum, $5D is cleared and the routine goes on. (A negative $57, which only the hard-landing path at $A50B can produce, is treated as airborne too.) Grounded, $5F is set when the world X $55/$56 lies in the base window $1261 to $1293 - the helicopter starts each sortie at $1273, in the middle of it. Then the settle counter: if $62 is already running control goes to $A875; else if $61 is set - the helicopter has been hit or reached - the counter is started at $A8A3 with $61 = $62 = 1; else the horizontal velocity decides, $5E being set at $A8AA when the machine is stopped and level and the counter being started when the speed is still at the clamped maximum of exactly +/-$1500 on touchdown. Flying at full speed in the air never reaches this test, because the airborne branch has already returned.
airborne: $5D set, and the 'stopped' and 'over the base' flags dropped
on the ground: $5D cleared, then the base window test for $5F
$5F = 1: world X is inside the base window $1261..$1293

Runs once a frame while the settle counter $62 is counting from 1 to 6. Below 6 it only increments; meanwhile $AFE5 subtracts $62 from the drawn altitude so the helicopter visibly sinks, $ABB2 hands it to $8BAF, which leaves it in $25 for the blitter, and $AC1B and $AC7B freeze both rotors. On the frame it reaches 6 the payoff fires once, guarded by $63: $63 is set, which takes lateral control away at $A74E, forces a descent at $A733 and starts the roughly 43-frame countdown at $968E that ends the sortie; $0CF1 is added in binary-coded decimal to the spade counter $0CFC by $A6E5, with its four-note figure, and to the running total $0CEF; $0CF1 is then zeroed and the diamond counter $0CFE cleared by $A6D2. $61, the flag that starts all this, is set in two places: $A8A3 just below, and $B5AF, which the collision code reaches when something comes within about twelve world units of the helicopter while it is on the ground.
start the settle counter: $61 and $62 both to 1 - reached from $A832 when the helicopter has been hit, or on touchdown at exactly full horizontal speed
$5E = 1 only when the helicopter is stopped and level, which is the condition the rest of the game tests for 'parked'

Applies a new bank angle to the helicopter; entered as a tail call from $A5B9 with the angle in A, and also stores it in $0B5F. The eleven side-view frames (shapes 0 to 10) are not drawn about a common centre, so the world position is corrected as the frame changes: the X anchor table $945B, read as words at 2*(bank+5) and giving +6,+5,+3,+2,0,0,-1,-2,-4,-5,-7 for bank -5 to +5, and the Y anchor table $9471, giving 7 to 10, are each differenced between the new angle and the old one and added to $55/$56 and $57, so the picture does not jump when the frame changes. Both offsets are mirrored when the helicopter faces left. $5A is then set to the new angle.

Returns a pseudo-random byte in A: the low byte of CIA1's free-running timer A, $DC04. This and the identical read at $9239 are the game's only source of randomness; callers include the hostage placement loop at $BE9E, the tank's decision at $B837 and the wreck shape choice at $B059.

Takes the actor in $72 off the active list and pushes it onto the free list. $0B7C,x is the backward link and $0B7D,x the forward one: the two neighbours are joined to each other, then the slot's forward link is made to point at the old free-list head $74 and $74 is set to the slot. Called with jsr from every actor that removes itself and from the collision code at $B3E1. Confirmed live: firing six shots produced six $A951 hits and five $A937 hits as the shots expired.

Takes the first slot off the free list: $72 = $74, then $74 = $0B7D of that slot. There is no empty check - the game relies on the 28 spare records $A9E1 chains never running out, and on the caps that limit each actor kind (at most five shots, for instance, enforced at $97E1). The caller then fills in the ten-byte record at $0B74 plus the slot and calls $A95B to put it on the active list.

Appends the slot in $72 to the end of the active actor list. The absolute cell $0B7C holds the index of the current last slot: the new slot becomes its forward link ($0B7D), $0B7C is updated to the new slot, the new slot's backward link is set to the old tail and its forward link to zero. If $73 - the slot $B307 means to visit next - is zero, it is pointed at the new slot, so an actor created part-way through the walk is still run this frame.

Redraws one two-digit status-bar counter. A holds the packed BCD value and X the counter number 0 to 2; $A99D gives the screen offset of the units digit. Both text matrices are written, $0450,y and $4450,y, because the top bar is double-buffered along with the bitmap, and each nibble is turned into a screen code by adding $30. Does nothing at all while bit 7 of $8C is clear, which is how the bar stays blank outside play.

Screen offsets, counted from $0450 (text row 2, column 0), of the units digit of the three status-bar counters: $0A for the spade counter $0CFC, $15 for the diamond counter $0CFE and $20 for the heart counter $0CFD. $A978 writes the units digit there and the tens digit one cell to its left; $BB2B stamps the spade, diamond and heart symbols one cell further left again, at $0458, $0463 and $046E.

Works out where a shape is to be drawn for the actor whose slot is in $72, and is the step every shape goes through before $8BF9. X is half the shape's width and Y half its height plus whatever extra vertical offset the caller wants. The destination comes back in $67/$68 - the 16-bit world X of the shape's left edge, the actor's world X $0B78/$0B79 minus X with X sign-extended - and $69, the row, which is the actor's field +6 ($0B7A) plus its field +7 ($0B7B) plus Y and is counted upward from the bottom of the play area, 0 at the bottom and $A7 at the top. A non-zero A asks for multicolour alignment: $67 is stepped on by one when ($67 xor the camera X $75) is odd, so the shape lands on a whole two-bit pixel. The caller then hands $0067 to $8BF9 and the shape pointer to $8BE0 before calling $8F03.

Builds the actor system from nothing; called from $BEF1 when a sortie starts. Empties both colour-overlay lists ($9D and $9E) and points $99/$9A and $9B/$9C at their buffers $0D03 and $0DA3. Record 0 at $0B74 is a dummy list head: its forward link ($0B7D read as an absolute address) and the tail cell ($0B7C read the same way) are both set to slot 10, which is filled in as the player - type 0, field +7 = $16, both links zero. Slots 20, 30, ... 290 are then chained through their forward links into the free list headed by $74, which gives 28 spare ten-byte records running up to $0C9F. Finally clears $0CE1, $0CE3 and $0CE8, the counts of the three short index lists.

Appends one record to this frame's colour-overlay list, which $BBE6 and $BC05 replay once the bitmap is finished to paint colour RAM. A is the stripe class, which $BC1D turns into a width and a height through the table at $94AF. Four bytes go to ($99),$9D: the class, then the screen X as a 16-bit value ($67/$68 minus the camera $75/$76), then the row $69; $9D is advanced by four. Every shape that wants colour calls this next to its blit - the helicopter with class 0, the hills with class 1, the jet with class 7 plus $9487[8*state + frame shape].

Draws the distant hills along the horizon; called once a frame from $95D4 and from the two other main loops. The screen X is taken from half the camera position - $75/$76 shifted right one with the low bit forced even - so the hills scroll at half the speed of the ground, which is the game's only parallax. Up to three copies of shape 64 (its pointer is the word at $8089) are laid side by side 256 pixels apart at row $1D, the ground line; a copy is skipped while its high byte $6E is below 4, which keeps the hills out of the left-hand end of the world. Each copy that is drawn queues colour stripe class 1 through $AA38 and blits with $8FD3. $0B60 counts the three copies down. Confirmed live: one hit per frame, in step with $AAC2.
inline argument: the destination $67/$68/$69 - world X of the left edge and the row

Continuation of $AA67 across the inline word at $AAA1: hands $8BE0 the pointer-table slot $8089, so $37/$38 ends up holding shape 64, the hill silhouette. The two bytes at $AAA6 are that routine's inline argument, not an instruction.
inline argument: $8089, the pointer-table slot for shape 64, the hill silhouette

Continuation of $AA67 across the inline word at $AAA6: clips this hill copy with $8F03 and, if any of it is on screen, queues colour stripe class 1 through $AA38 and blits with $8FD3. Then steps $68 and $6E on by one, which moves the next copy 256 pixels to the right, and loops until the counter $0B60 has drawn three.

Draws the helicopter body and is the front end of the whole shape-drawing sequence; called from $AFEF. It picks a shape and a blitter from the yaw $59 (-3 full left, 0 head-on, +3 full right), the bank $5A and the hard-contact flag $60. Shape choice goes through the pointer table at $8009, 75 interleaved lo/hi words, read here at $AB4C/$AB52 and at $AB69/$AB6E. Fully side-on and banked uses shapes 0 to 10, indexed by 5 plus the bank signed by the facing, so 5 is the level frame. Fully side-on, level, on the one frame the skids bite ($60 set) uses shape 14 through $8025; head-on and level on that frame uses shape 15 through $8027. Everything else uses shape 11 plus |yaw| - 11, 12 or 13 - and is sheared rather than pre-drawn: $8C30 is called with the signed bank to load the shear slope $2B/$2C from $8C48 (one row every 3 to 13 columns), and $927E, indexed by 5*(bank+5) + yaw + 2, supplies an extra vertical offset in $6F. The blitter goes into $7F/$80: $8FD3 plain when level and facing right, $903E mirrored when level and facing left, otherwise the entry from $ABBF at 2*(yaw+3). Then the standard draw: half the shape's width (byte 0 of the shape, halved, because it is a bit count and the bitmap is multicolour) in X, half its height plus $6F in Y, $A9A0 to turn those into $67/$68/$69 from the player's actor record, $8BF9 with the inline word $0067 to copy that into $34/$35/$36, $8BE0 with the inline word $0065 to copy the shape pointer into $37/$38, $8F03 to clip and set up, $8BAF handed the settle counter $62 (it leaves it in $25 with $22-$24 cleared; what the blitter does with $25 is outside this range), and finally the chosen blitter reached by pushing $ABBD and doing jmp ($7F), which returns to the rts at $ABBE.
shape 15: head-on, level, on the frame the skids bite
shape 14: full side view, level, on the frame the skids bite
shape index 5 + signed bank: the eleven side-view frames 0..10
shape index 11 + |yaw|: head-on and the two turning frames, drawn sheared
inline argument: the destination $67/$68/$69 the call to $A9A0 just computed
inline argument: $0065, holding the helicopter body shape chosen above
call the blitter chosen in $7F/$80; the pushed $ABBD makes it return to the rts at $ABBE

Low bytes of the seven blitter entry points $AAC2 chooses between when the helicopter is banked, indexed by 2*($59+3) for yaw -3 to +3: $903E, $90DF, $90DF, $90D2, $90D2, $90D2, $8FD3. $903E draws mirrored and $8FD3 plain; $90D2 and $90DF are the pair that apply the shear $8C30 set up, which is why they serve the turning frames.
High bytes of those same seven blitter addresses; $AAF4 and $AAF9 read $ABBF,y and $ABC0,y as one little-endian pointer into $7F/$80.

Draws the main rotor disc over the helicopter; called from $AFF2. The offset from the body is the sum of two tables: $92B5, indexed by 14*(bank+5) + 2*(yaw+3), gives a small per-facing correction in $86/$87, and $934F/$9350, indexed by 2*(bank+5), gives the base offset - about 16 to the left and 6 up when level. $A9A0 turns that into the destination and $8BF9 with the inline word $0067 stores it; $8C30 is then called with the bank so the disc is sheared exactly as the body is. The phase counter $0B61 steps 4, 2, 0 and wraps, choosing one of shapes 16, 17 and 18 through $8029 + $0B61, and is held at 4 whenever the settle counter $62 is running, so the rotor stops turning as the machine settles. $8BE0 with the inline word $0065 loads the shape, $8F03 clips and $90D2 blits.
inline argument: the destination $67/$68/$69 of the rotor disc
rotor blur shapes 16, 17, 18 by phase $0B61
inline argument: $0065, holding the rotor blur shape for phase $0B61

Draws the tail rotor; called from $AFF5. Returns at once unless the helicopter is fully side-on ($59 = +3 or -3), because the tail only shows in profile. The offset comes from $9365 when facing right - x +18 or +19, y +1 to +11 - or $937B when facing left - x -12 or -13 - indexed by 2*(bank+5), so the tail follows the body's pitch. The phase counter $0B62 steps 6, 4, 2, 0 and wraps, choosing one of shapes 19 to 22 through $802F + $0B62, and like the main rotor is frozen at 6 while the settle counter $62 runs. $8BE0 with the inline word $0065 takes the shape, $A9A0 and $8BF9 with the inline word $0067 the position, then $8F03 clips and $8FD3 blits.
tail rotor shapes 19..22 by phase $0B62
inline argument: $0065, holding the tail-rotor shape for phase $0B62

Continuation of $AC4A across the inline word at $ACA0: puts the tail-rotor offset just read from $9365 or $937B into X and Y and calls $A9A0, which turns it into the destination $67/$68/$69 relative to the player's actor record.
inline argument: the destination $67/$68/$69 of the tail rotor

Continuation of $AC4A across the inline word at $ACAE: clips the tail rotor with $8F03 and, when it is on screen, blits it plain with $8FD3. No colour stripe is queued for it - the helicopter's single class-0 stripe covers the whole machine.

Gives back the position of the helicopter's gun muzzle relative to the machine's own centre: the horizontal offset in X and the vertical one in Y, read as a pair from $9391 at 14*(bank+5) + 2*(yaw+3) - one entry for each of the eleven bank angles crossed with the seven yaw stages. The offsets run from about +14 when head-on to -15 when fully side-on. Called from $B019 the instant a shot is created; confirmed live, hit exactly once per shot fired.

An eight-bit shift-and-add multiply: $7D times $7E, product low byte left in $7F and high byte in A and $80, twenty bytes ending in rts. Nothing in $8000-$BFFF refers to it - no cross-reference, and a checkpoint on it was never hit during play - so it is left-over library code that the build kept.

Arithmetic shift right of the signed 16-bit value in $7F/$80 by Y places. The value is made positive on the way in, shifted Y times, and negated again on the way out, so the sign is preserved; Y is never zero at any call site. This is the game's only division, and the flight model leans on it: drag at $A41D with Y = 4, velocity into movement at $A64A and $A6A4 with Y = 8, the skid at $A535 with Y = 1, the bank calculation at $A58C with Y = 9, the camera look-ahead at $BD22 with Y = 5.

Fills in a new shot's motion fields from the helicopter's attitude; called from $B048 with the new slot in $72. The byte pair at $942B, indexed by 12*|yaw| + 2*|bank|, gives the shot's speed. Field +1 ($0B75) is the horizontal step - negated when the helicopter faces left, then offset by the helicopter's own horizontal speed (the high byte of $51/$52, rounded toward zero) so shots inherit the machine's momentum. Field +2 ($0B76) is the vertical step, negated when yaw and bank have opposite signs. Field +3 ($0B77) comes from $AD86 indexed by |yaw|. Head-on shots barely move sideways at all (0 to 2 a frame) while fully side-on shots cross the screen at 26.
The value $AD24 puts in a new shot's field +3 ($0B77), indexed by |yaw| 0 to 3: $FE, $FE, $FF, $00 - so the flatter the shot, the closer to zero. The type-6 handler at $B16E is what reads it back.

How many animation frames each of the jet's five states lasts, read at $AF6F and $AF8F: state 0 never ends (0), state 1 runs 18 frames, state 2 runs 15, and states 3 and 4 run 10 each. When the jet's field +2 reaches the count for its state, the state is over.

Actor handler 9, the enemy jet - entry 9 of the dispatch table at $B32E; the shapes it draws (indices 23, 24, 31 and 36 upward in the $8009 table) render as an aircraft in profile and three-quarter view. Field +1 is the state (0 cruising, 1 and 2 the two attack manoeuvres, 3 and 4 the firing run) and field +2 the frame within it. The state selects an animation script through the pointer table at $AFC2/$AFC3 ($94E3, $94E7, $952F, $956B, $956B) and a shape base through $AFCC/$AFCD ($8037, $8039, $8047, $8051, $8051). Each script entry is four bytes: a shape sub-index kept in $0B51, a horizontal step and two vertical steps; state 0 is a single frame that simply moves the jet 8 units a frame. Drawing uses the standard sequence - $8BE0 with the inline word $0065 for the shape, $A9A0 with A = 1 so the jet is snapped to the multicolour pixel grid, $8BF9 with the inline word $0067 for the destination, $8F03 to clip - then $8FD3 plain or $903E mirrored according to the sign of field +3. $0B50 is set to $FF before the clip and cleared only if the jet was on screen. An on-screen jet also queues a colour stripe of class 7 + $9487[8*state + sub-index]. The script's steps are then applied to fields +6, +7 and +4/+5 (the horizontal one negated when the jet faces left), and in states 1 and 2 field +6 is dragged to within $1E of the helicopter's altitude $57. The state machine last: state 0 begins a manoeuvre when the helicopter is near enough - the reach is $98 + 4*$8D, so it grows with the counter $8D - choosing state 1 or state 2 from whether the helicopter's heading ($52) and the jet's facing (field +3) agree and from how fast the helicopter is moving; it goes straight to state 4, frame 5, if the helicopter has already been hit ($61) or if the jet is past world X $1100. States 1 and 2 count their frames out, flip the facing at the end of state 1, and then become state 3 if the helicopter is airborne or state 4 if it is on the ground. States 3 and 4 fire on their first frame - $B665 creates a pair of type-4 actors eight rows above and nine below the jet, $B6ED a single type-5 - and when their ten frames are up the jet takes itself off both the short list ($B5F5) and the actor list ($A937), but only if it had gone off screen.
inline argument: $0065, holding the jet shape the script picked

Continuation of $AD8F across the inline word at $ADDA: reads the jet shape's first two bytes, the width in bitmap bits and the height in rows, halves each (two bits are one multicolour pixel) into X and Y, and calls $A9A0 with A = 1 so the jet is snapped to the multicolour pixel grid.
inline argument: the destination $67/$68/$69 of the jet

Continuation of the jet handler $AD8F across the inline word at $ADF0, and the bulk of it. Sets $0B50 to $FF, clips with $8F03, and for an on-screen jet clears $0B50, blits plain ($8FD3) or mirrored ($903E) according to the sign of field +3, and queues colour stripe class 7 + $9487[8*state + shape sub-index]. Then applies the animation script's three steps to fields +6, +7 and +4/+5 (the horizontal one negated when the jet faces left); in states 1 and 2 it drags field +6 to within $1E of the helicopter's altitude $57. The rest is the state machine: state 0 decides whether to begin a manoeuvre, states 1 and 2 count their frames out and then pick the firing state from whether the helicopter is airborne, and states 3 and 4 fire on their first frame through $B665 or $B6ED and take the jet off the lists through $B5F5 and $A937 when they end.
colour stripe class 7 + $9487[8*state + sub-index]

Low bytes of the five animation-script pointers $AD8F uses, one per jet state: $94E3, $94E7, $952F, $956B, $956B (states 3 and 4 share a script). Each script is four bytes a frame - shape sub-index, horizontal step, field +6 step, field +7 step.
High bytes of the same five script pointers; $AD96 and $AD9B read $AFC2,y and $AFC3,y with y = 2*state as one little-endian word into $6F/$70.

Low bytes of the five shape-base pointers $AD8F uses, one per jet state: $8037, $8039, $8047, $8051, $8051. These are addresses inside the shape pointer table at $8009, so they name shape indices 23 (the cruising jet), 24, 31 and 36; the script's sub-index is added on top.
High bytes of the same five shape-base pointers; $ADBF and $ADC4 read $AFCC,y and $AFCD,y with y = 2*state into $6F/$70, and the sub-index in $0B51 then indexes that as a table of shape pointers.

Actor handler 0, the player's helicopter - entry 0 of the dispatch table at $B32E. First it copies the flight variables into the actor record so everything that reads actor records sees the machine where it is drawn: world X $55/$56 into fields +4/+5, the altitude $57 minus the settle counter $62 into field +6, and the constant ground base $58 (always $16) into field +7. Then it draws the machine in three pieces - $AAC2 the body, $ABCD the main rotor, $AC4A the tail rotor - and queues a colour stripe of class 0 at the actor's own position ($A9A0 with X and Y both zero, then $AA38 with A = 0); class 0 is the one case $BC29 special-cases, moving it $16 left and $0E up before it is painted. The routine then runs on past $B000, where it handles the fire button, the shot it creates at $B00F, the wreck animation while $61 is set, and finally the flight update $A4C7.
drawn altitude = $57 - $62, so the helicopter sinks while it settles

Second half of the actor handler for type 0, the player's helicopter, whose entry is $AFD6. $AFD6 copied the live machine's position into the actor record ($55/$56 world X, $57 height, $58 base row), drew it, and queued its dirty rectangle with size code 0 (7x23 cells). Here: if bit 7 of $64 is set, the fire button latched at $97E7, the flag is cleared, the shot is counted in $0CF3, $A951 takes a slot off the free list and it is made actor type 6. $ACB7 looks the muzzle offset up in the table at $9391 by the current aim pair ($59, $5A); that offset plus one is subtracted from the helicopter's world X and its Y part added to the height, the base row is copied from $58, $AD24 sets the shot's velocity and $A95B links it in. Then $B04E: with $61 clear the routine just falls out through $B0CE, otherwise the helicopter has been destroyed and $5D picks the airborne death at $B059 or the burning wreck at $B08D.

Death sequence for a helicopter destroyed while still in the air ($61 set, $5D = 1). $B059 has just picked one of the four explosion-cloud shapes, table entries 51 to 54 read through $806F, using $DC04 as the random source. Its header gives the width and height in bits and rows; half of each goes to $A9A0 so the cloud is centred on the helicopter and its world X rounded to an even bitmap column, and $8BF9 hands the position to the blitter. Continues at $B084.

Blits the random explosion cloud over the dying helicopter and returns through $B0CE. The carry from $8F03 is deliberately not tested and no $AA38 entry is made, because the helicopter's own dirty rectangle already covers the cloud. The other half of the death sequence is at $B08D, taken when the wreck is on the ground ($5D = 0): once a frame it allocates a slot, puts it eight world units to the left of the helicopter plus a random 0 to 15, at height 0 on base row $58, and $B2EA turns it into a ground burst, so the wreck goes on throwing up explosions. $B0CE then runs the helicopter's own flight model at $A4C7.

Adds one, in BCD, to the two-digit counter held in $0CFC and repaints it in the first field of the top bar through $A978, which writes screen $045A and $445A. The first call in a frame - $0D02 is zeroed once per frame at $9676 - also plays three falling notes on SID voice 3, $A7C7 with frequency high bytes $60, $54 and $39. Called from $B63E and from the identical code at $9E14, the two places a person in the $0CA0 array is killed. X and Y are saved in $84/$85.

Actor handler for types 1 and 2, the explosion cloud: type 1 is a burst in the air, type 2 a burst sitting on the ground, and $B2EA chooses between them from the height. $0B75 is the animation frame 0 to 3 and selects shape table entry 51 + frame through $806F, the four frames of the expanding and dissipating cloud. The type is compared with 2 and the flags pushed across the shape lookup, so that a ground burst gets four extra rows of lift and sits on the ground instead of half inside it. Continues at $B122.

Reads the chosen cloud's header: half its width in bitmap columns into X and half its height in rows into A, plus the four rows of lift for a ground burst, then $A9A0 with the align flag set turns that into a screen position centred on the actor and rounded to an even bitmap column so the multicolour pixels line up. $8BF9 passes the position on. Continues at $B13E.

Drops the SID master volume to 3 at $D418 unless $62 is 6, queues the dirty rectangle with size code 5 (5x12 cells), blits the cloud and puts the volume back to 15. That pair of writes happens once a frame for every explosion on screen and is the only sound this handler makes; the audible result is the click a bare write to the volume register produces, and why it is done from the drawing code rather than from the sound code is not clear. $0B75 is then advanced and on the fourth frame the actor unlinks itself through $A937.

Actor handler for type 6, a shot fired by the player's helicopter and created at $B008. Draws shape table entry 46, the two-pixel bullet, one bitmap column left of the actor and one row above it, with dirty-rectangle size code $0E. Continues at $B181.
Inline parameter of the $8BE0 call above: $37/$38 is loaded with the word at $8065, which is entry 46 of the shape table at $8009 and points at the bullet bitmap at $8812.

Moves and retires the player's shot. $B2AA is called with a fall rate of 0 when $0B77 is zero and 2 otherwise. $AD24 set $0B77 from the table at $AD86 indexed by the magnitude of $59, the helicopter's turn position, which runs -3 to +3 with 0 the head-on view; the values are -2, -2, -1, 0, so only a shot fired with the machine fully side on ($59 = +/-3) flies level and keeps its base row. Every other shot loses one or two rows of base row per frame as well as falling, and the moment its $0B7B stops matching $58 the collision test at $B344 rejects it on its first line: that is how shots fired while the helicopter is turned towards the viewer hit nothing. Watching a shot fired head-on in the emulator shows exactly that, $0B77 = $FE with the base row walking down 2 a frame. The shot is discarded if its world X high byte has left the helicopter's by more than one (the compare at $B19F has no preceding sec, so the difference can be one out), its base row is clamped up to 3, and the height then decides: under 4 or wrapped past $E0 it explodes on the ground unless it is already at base row 3, over $90 it is simply thrown away, and in between it goes to $B344 to look for a target. Every exit decrements the in-flight count $0CF3.

Actor handler for type 5, the single shell a jet lobs when the helicopter is on the ground; $B6ED creates it. Draws shape table entry 49, a flat four-pixel bar, four bitmap columns left of the actor, with dirty-rectangle size code $10. Continues at $B1FA.
Inline parameter of the $8BE0 call above: $37/$38 is loaded with the word at $806B, entry 49 of the shape table, the flat bar at $8824.

Steps the jet's shell with a fall rate of 4, the heaviest in the game, so it drops steeply. The shell has no collision test of its own; the only thing that happens to it is that its height wraps past $A0, whereupon the height is zeroed, $B2EA turns it into a ground explosion and $B4AF works out what that burst lands on. Since $B4AF only hurts the helicopter when $5D says it is on the ground, this shell can kill only a landed machine, which is exactly the case in which the jet chooses to fire it.

Actor handler for type 4, one of the pair of rockets a jet fires head on while the helicopter is airborne; $B665 creates two at a time, one above and one below the aircraft. Draws shape table entry 48, a five-pixel finned round, four bitmap columns left of the actor and one row up, with dirty-rectangle size code $0F, blitted mirrored through $903E when the horizontal velocity $0B75 is negative so the rocket points the way it is going. Continues at $B233.
Inline parameter of the $8BE0 call above: $37/$38 is loaded with the word at $8069, entry 48 of the shape table, the finned round at $881C.

Steps the rocket with a fall rate of 1, so it flies almost flat at its 24 world units a frame, then tests it against the helicopter at $B433 while its height is between 3 and $9F. Outside that band the height is zeroed, $B2EA turns the rocket into a ground explosion and $B4AF decides what the burst hit.

Actor handler for type 8, the arcing shell. Two things fire it: a tank, at $A2C4, which launches it one row above and one base row in front of itself with a velocity triple taken from the tables at $A354, $A359 and $A35E, and the homing mine at $B848, which lets one go straight down. Draws shape table entry 47, a one-pixel vertical dash, on the actor's own position with dirty-rectangle size code $0D. Continues at $B27E.
Inline parameter of the $8BE0 call above: $37/$38 is loaded with the word at $8067, entry 47 of the shape table, the vertical dash at $8817.

Steps the shell with a fall rate of 3. Because $B2AA also adds $0B77 to the base row every frame, a tank's shell climbs out of the tanks' rows, 5 to 12, towards the helicopter's plane at $58 = 22 as it travels, which is how the game fakes depth. The shell itself tests nothing: when its height reaches zero or goes negative it is snapped to height 0 on base row $58, $B2EA turns it into a ground explosion and $B4AF takes over.

One frame of ballistic movement for the actor whose slot is in $72, with the fall rate in A. Adds the signed horizontal velocity $0B75 to the 16-bit world X in $0B78/$0B79, adds the vertical velocity $0B76 to the height $0B7A and the depth step $0B77 to the base row $0B7B - the two vertical fields are kept apart here and added together again by $A9A0 to give the bitmap row - and finally takes A off the vertical velocity so the actor falls. A is parked in $0B63. Heights count upwards from the bottom of the play area, because the row pointer table at $0A00/$0AA8 runs bottom to top.

Turns the actor in $72 into an explosion in place, keeping its slot, its world X and its links. Clears both velocities $0B75 and $0B76 and sets the type to 1 when the height $0B7A is non-zero, a burst in the air, or to 2 when it is zero, a burst on the ground which $B106 lifts four rows. Every projectile in the game ends this way rather than by unlinking itself.

Walks the actor list once and runs a handler for each entry; called from $95DA once a frame and again from $96D5 and $972D. $0B7D read as a plain address is the head slot and $0B7D,x the link to the next; $0B7C,x is the back link that $A937 needs to unlink one. The next slot is copied into $73 before the handler runs so that a handler may destroy its own actor. The type in $0B74,x indexes the split address table at $B32E/$B32F, and $B328 is pushed as the return address before the indirect jump, so every handler just ends in rts and arrives at $B329.
Where a handler's rts lands, one byte on from the $B328 that $B307 pushed. Picks the next slot out of $73 and loops back to $B30A, or returns when the link is zero and the list is done.

Low bytes of the eleven actor handler addresses, read at $B316 with 2*type in Y. In order: 0 $AFD6 the player's helicopter, 1 and 2 $B106 the explosion in the air and on the ground, 3 $A0BB the tank, 4 $B221 the jet's rocket, 5 $B1E8 the jet's shell, 6 $B16E the helicopter's own shot, 7 $0000, which is never reached because nothing is ever given type 7, 8 $B26D the arcing shell, 9 $AD8F the jet, 10 $B73D the homing mine.
High bytes of the same eleven handler addresses, read at $B31B. The table is interleaved low byte then high byte, so these two symbols are the alternate bytes of $B32E to $B343.

Works out what the player's shot in $72 has hit; reached from $B1C9 while its height is between 4 and $8F. It gives up at once unless the shot is still on the helicopter's own base row $58, which is what makes shots fired into the screen harmless. Below height $0E it tests the four 24-unit boxes at world X $0380, $0480, $0580 and $0680, the sheds, and blows the shot up there. From height $18 up it walks the jets whose slots are listed in $0CE4 with the count in $0CE3: a jet is hit when its base row is within 8 above $58, the heights are within 8 rows and the world X within 19 bitmap columns, and $B3E1 then kills the shot and sends the jet to $B61F. Last, if a homing mine is alive ($0CE1 set, slot in $0CE2), the same test with a box of +/-16 columns and +/-8 rows sends it to $B630.

Tests a jet's rocket against the helicopter: height within 9 rows of $57 and world X within 10 bitmap columns of $55/$56. On a hit the rocket is dropped to one below the helicopter's base row, $B2EA turns it into an explosion and $B5AF marks the helicopter destroyed. This and the mine at $B474 are the only two ways the machine can be shot down in the air; everything else has to catch it on the ground through $B4AF.

Tests the homing mine against the helicopter, a wider box than the rocket's: height within 7 rows of $57 and world X within 18 bitmap columns of $55/$56. A hit first clears $0CE1 so the scheduler may send another mine, then joins the rocket's code at $B466 to explode the mine and destroy the helicopter.

Decides what an actor that has just been turned into an explosion landed on. Nothing at all happens once its world X high byte reaches $12, off the end of the map. A burst below the helicopter's plane (base row under $58) goes to $B552 and is tested against the tanks. A burst at or above that plane destroys the helicopter if the helicopter is on the ground ($5D = 0) and within 11 bitmap columns, then walks all sixteen four-byte records of the people array at $0CA0, skipping any already flagged dead in +0 and any whose state in +1 is 2 or $FE, and kills anyone within 10 columns through $B63E. The subtraction at $B50E has no preceding sec, so that horizontal comparison is computed one unit short. Finally, a burst inside one of the 24-unit boxes at world X $0380, $0480 or $0580 goes to $B652 and opens that shed.

Tests an explosion that went off below the helicopter's plane against the tanks, whose slots are listed in $0CE9 with the count in $0CE8. A tank counts as hit when its base row is within about ten of the explosion's and its world X within 13 bitmap columns; the explosion then unlinks itself through $A937 and $B5BB destroys the tank.

Marks the player's helicopter as destroyed. Sets $61, which makes the type-0 handler run the death sequence at $B055 from the next frame on, and sets $0B76 of the actor that did the killing to 4. Called from $B471 when a rocket or the mine connects, and from $B4E3 and $B4EF when a ground explosion catches a landed machine.

Destroys the tank whose position in the $0CE9 list is in A: points $72 at the tank's slot, $B2EA turns it into an explosion, the tank count $0CE8 drops by one and the list is compacted by falling into $B5D1. $72 is left pointing at the tank, not at the explosion that killed it.

Takes the slot in $72 out of the four-entry tank list at $0CE9 to $0CEC by shifting the later entries down, and drops the count $0CE8. Called from $A16B when a tank leaves the map, and entered one instruction in, at $B5D1, from $B5BB when one is blown up.

Takes the slot in $72 out of the four-entry jet list at $0CE4 to $0CE7 and drops the count $0CE3. Called from $AF7F when a jet finishes its attack run and leaves, and entered at $B5FA from $B61F when one is shot down. The later entries are shifted down so the order of the surviving jets is kept.
Destroys the jet whose position in the $0CE4 list is in A: points $72 at the jet's slot, $B2EA turns it into an explosion, the jet count $0CE3 drops by one and the list is compacted through $B5FA.
Destroys the homing mine. Its slot is in $0CE2, $B2EA turns it into an explosion, and $0CE1 is cleared so the scheduler at $A38C is free to release another one.

Kills the person whose record index is in Y: flags $0CA0,y with $FF, counts one more lost in $0CEF and one fewer outside in $0CF0, and scores it through $B0D2. Leaves the killing actor's $0B76 at 3, which is also what makes the caller's loop at $B534 continue. The same three lines appear at $9E14 for the other way a person can die.

Opens the shed whose index is in A by setting $0CF4,x to 1, which is what lets the release code at $9E49 start sending that shed's people out, and sets the exploding actor's $0B76 to 2. Does nothing if the shed is already open. The box test that reaches here, at $B54B, admits indices 0 to 2 only, while the matching test for a shot at $B369 admits 0 to 3; the fourth shed is opened anyway before play starts, because $BE63 writes 1 into $0CF7, so the difference does not show.

Fires the jet's pair of rockets. Called from $AF5B when the jet is in state 3, the state it uses while the helicopter is in the air. Allocates two slots, makes both type 4, puts them on the jet's world X eight rows above and nine rows below it, roughly the wingtips of the head-on aircraft, both on the helicopter's base row $58, and gives both 24 world units a frame in the direction bit 7 of the jet's $0B77 is facing. $72 is saved in $0B64 and $0B65 and restored, so the jet's own handler carries on undisturbed.

Fires the jet's single shell. Called from $AF61 when the jet is in state 4, the state it uses while the helicopter is on the ground. Allocates one slot, makes it type 5, puts it on the jet's world X one row below it on base row $58, and gives it 20 world units a frame in the direction bit 7 of the jet's $0B77 is facing. $72 is saved in $0B64 and restored.

Actor handler for type 10, the single homing enemy the scheduler at $A38C releases from the third sortie onwards ($8D of 2 or more, one at a time, its slot in $0CE2 and its presence in $0CE1). $A044 launches it about 440 world units to one side of the helicopter at height $70. Draws shape table entry 50, a small blocky object ten rows tall, six bitmap columns left and seven rows above the actor position, with dirty-rectangle size code $19; it is blitted plain or mirrored on alternate frames according to bit 0 of the frame counter $89, so it looks as though it is turning, and on each of those frames it sounds one of two pitches on SID voice 3 through $A7C7 ($F0 or $FF), the warble that warns the player. $0B67 is set to $FF when it was actually drawn and $0B77 counts frames 0, 1, 2. Continues at $B755.
Inline parameter of the $8BE0 call above: $37/$38 is loaded with the word at $806D, entry 50 of the shape table, the mine bitmap at $8827.

Blits the mine and then steers it. It is abandoned, and $0CE1 cleared, as soon as the helicopter's world X high byte is more than two away from its own, which is what stops mines following the player across the whole map. Otherwise it chases: the horizontal velocity $0B75 is moved one unit a frame towards the helicopter and clamped to +/-5, and while the mine is on screen the vertical velocity $0B76 is moved towards the helicopter's height and clamped to +/-1; off screen it stops climbing. $B2AA is then called with no fall rate and with $0B77 held at zero over the call, so the mine neither falls nor drifts out of its plane. On the last sortie ($8D = 3) a mine that is on screen, below height $58, on the frame its 0-2 counter is zero and one time in four on the random byte from $DC04, drops a type-8 shell at its own position with its own horizontal speed plus or minus 10 and sounds a note. Height above $A0 or below $0A ends the mine as a ground explosion through $B2EA and $B4AF; in between, $B474 tests it against the helicopter. The routine runs on past $B7FF and ends at $B80A.

Tail of the actor handler entered at $B73D (type 10 in the $B32E dispatch table; the entry itself is outside this range). Steps the actor with $B2AA while field +3 ($0B77,x) is held aside and the gravity term is zero, so this actor keeps a constant velocity for the frame, then puts field +3 back. It then fires: when the phase byte $8D is 3, field +3 is zero, the 'was drawn this frame' flag $0B67 is set, the actor's height $0B7A,x is below $58 and a fresh CIA1 timer sample from $A933 has bits 3 and 6 both clear (about one frame in four), $A951 takes a slot off the free list and fills it as a type 8 actor at the parent's 16-bit X ($0B78/$0B79) and height ($0B7A), with $0B7B from zero page $58, an X velocity of the parent's plus or minus $0A chosen by bit 7 of the random byte, both velocity fractions cleared, links it into the live list with $A95B and plays a short blip ($A7C7, X=$78, Y=1). Finally, if the actor's height has left the band $0A..$9F it is zeroed, $0CE1 is cleared and $B2EA stops the actor (turning it into type 1 or 2) before continuing at $B4AF; otherwise the handler carries on at $B474.

Draws the four prisoner sheds, once per frame, from the startup and play loops at $96C3 and $9727. Returns immediately unless the camera high byte $76 is $03..$06, the only stretch of the world the sheds occupy. The sheds stand at fixed world X $037D, $047D, $057D and $067D - 256 units apart, hard coded here, not read from any table - with the low bit of the X taken from the camera's low bit so the multicolour pixel pairs never straddle. $0B69 counts the shed 0..3, $0B6A/$0B6B holds its world X and $0B6B is bumped by one per shed. For each: body at bitmap row $24 (36), ground bar at row $19 (25), and for a shed already blown open a small figure in the doorway six units right at row $1C (28). Reads the per-shed state array $0CF4..$0CF7 (0 = intact, 1 = open) and the shape pointer table at $8009.
the draw position triple at $0067: X low, X high, bitmap row

Picks the shed's body shape from its state: $0CF4,x is 0 while the shed is intact and 1 once it has been blown open, and doubles into the interleaved shape pointer table, reaching entry 71 or entry 72 through $8097/$8098. Both are 27 bits by 11 rows. Leaves the chosen pointer in $65/$66 for the $8BE0 that follows.
$0065, the scratch word holding the shed body's shape pointer

Clips the shed body against the scroll window with $8F03 and blits it with $8FD3 when any of it is on screen. Then drops the draw row to $19 (25) and reloads the position triple, ready for the solid bar of ground the shed stands on.
the draw position triple at $0067, now with row $19
Loads the pointer to shape 73, the 27-bit by 2-row solid bar of ground a shed stands on, into $37/$38 from the shape table entry at $809B. Three bytes of jsr wedged between two inline word arguments.
$809B: shape table entry 73, the 27-bit by 2-row solid ground bar

Draws the bar of ground under a shed and books the shed's erase rectangle. If $8F03 reports the bar fully off screen the whole shed is skipped. Otherwise the row goes back to $24 (36) and $AA38 records one rectangle for the next pass of $BBE6 under code $17, whose size comes from $94AF+2*$17: 5 character columns by 13 bitmap rows, enough to cover the body and the bar together. An intact shed ($0CF4,x = 0) is then finished; an open one also gets a figure in the doorway, six units right at row $1C.
the draw position triple at $0067, six units right of the shed
Loads the pointer to shape 74, the 15-bit by 3-row figure that appears in the doorway of a shed that has been blown open, into $37/$38 from the shape table entry at $809D.
$809D: shape table entry 74, the 15-bit by 3-row doorway figure

Draws the figure in an opened shed's doorway, flipping it left and right every frame: bit 0 of the frame counter $89 chooses between the plain blit $8FD3 and the mirrored blit $903E. Then the loop tail advances $0B69 to the next shed, adds one to the world-X high byte $0B6B so the next shed is 256 units further right, and goes back to $B8D2, stopping after four.

Draws four small scenery objects in front of the home base at four different parallax rates, from the play loops at $96C0 and $9724. Returns unless the camera high byte $76 is $10, $11 or $12. The anchor is world X $1174 (low bit matched to the camera's). It forms E = ($1174 - camera - $8C) rounded down to even, then halves it three times with the signed shift $ACF1 to fill four world X values at $0B6C, $0B6E, $0B70 and $0B72: $1174 + E/8, + E/4, + E/2 and + E. Because $8F03 subtracts the camera again, their screen positions move at 1.125, 1.25, 1.5 and 2 times the camera's rate, so the four fan out as the helicopter flies. Their bitmap rows come from $BA3B: 28, 26, 23 and 16, highest for the slowest, so they read as depth over the ground. All four use shape 70, a 4-pixel by 5-row blob; what the blob is meant to be is not settled by the code.
the draw position triple at $0067 for one parallax object
Loads the pointer to shape 70, the 4-pixel by 5-row blob used for all four parallax scenery objects, into $37/$38 from the shape table entry at $8095. Reached once per object, four times a frame.
$8095: shape table entry 70, the 4-pixel by 5-row blob

Draws one parallax object and books its erase rectangle. Y (0..3) selects the object and is saved across the call; $AA38 code $16 gives a 2-column by 5-row rectangle from $94AF. Off-screen objects are skipped without booking anything. Four passes, then rts.

The bitmap row of each of the four parallax scenery objects, slowest first: $1C, $1A, $17, $10 - rows 28, 26, 23 and 16 counting up from the bottom of the play area. Four entries, one byte each, read only at $BA15 with Y = the object index 0..3.

Draws the home base, the fixed structure at the right-hand end of the world. Called from every draw sequence: $95D7, $965A, $96BD, $9721, $974F and $9761. Returns unless the camera high byte $76 is $11 or $12. The base sits at world X $1254, hard coded here, with the low bit copied from the camera so multicolour pixel pairs stay aligned; $78/$79 holds it. Built from six pieces, bottom to top: a solid apron 15 columns by 5 rows at X+$0F row $19 (from the fill record at $BB25, painted with $8C5E, not the shape blitter); shape 66, an 8 by 5 sloping wedge, mirrored at X-1 and plain at X+$7F so the two face outward $80 units apart; shape 65, a 13 by 11 bunker half, plain at X+$48 and mirrored at X+$62 to make one symmetrical building at row $22 (34); shape 67, the 1-pixel by 12-row flagpole at X+$71 row $2E (46); and the flag, shape 68 or 69 chosen by bit 0 of the frame counter $89 so it waves. Erase rectangles are booked through $AA38 under codes $13, $14 and $15.
the draw position triple at $0067: base X + $0F, row $19

One of only two calls to $8BBA in the whole program, the inline routine that takes a literal 16-bit value rather than a pointer: it leaves $37/$38 holding $BB25 itself, the address of the base apron's fill record.
the literal value $BB25 - one of only two $8BBA sites; $37/$38 is left pointing at the local fill record there, not at a shape

Paints the base's solid apron with $8C5E when $8F03 says any of it is on screen: 15 character columns by 5 bitmap rows of pattern $AA, i.e. multicolour colour 2 throughout, from the record at $BB25. Then steps the position one unit left of the base anchor for the left-hand wedge.
the draw position triple at $0067: base X - 1, row $19
Loads the pointer to shape 66, the 8-pixel by 5-row sloping wedge that caps each end of the base, into $37/$38 from the shape table entry at $808D. Both wedges use it, one mirrored.
$808D: shape table entry 66, the 8-pixel by 5-row sloping wedge

Draws the left-hand wedge of the base mirrored ($903E) at base X - 1, row $19, after booking erase code $13 - 22 columns by 5 rows, the widest rectangle the game uses, covering the apron and both wedges at once. If the wedge is off screen the rest of the base is abandoned. Then moves the position to base X + $7F for the matching right-hand wedge.

Draws the same wedge shape unmirrored ($8FD3) at base X + $7F, so the two slopes face outward $80 units apart and frame the apron. No erase rectangle of its own: code $13 already covers it. Then sets row $22 (34) and position base X + $48 for the bunker.
the draw position triple at $0067: base X + $48, row $22
Loads the pointer to shape 65, the 13-pixel by 11-row bunker half, into $37/$38 from the shape table entry at $808B. Drawn twice, plain and mirrored, to make the whole building.
$808B: shape table entry 65, the 13-pixel by 11-row bunker half
Books erase code $14 (9 columns by 9 rows) and blits the left half of the bunker at base X + $48, row $22. Then advances the position $1A units for its mirror image.

Draws the second half of the bunker mirrored ($903E) $1A units right of the first, which is what makes the building symmetrical from one 13-pixel shape. Then sets row $2E (46) and position base X + $71 for the flagpole.
the draw position triple at $0067: base X + $71, row $2E
Loads the pointer to shape 67, the 1-pixel wide, 12-row flagpole, into $37/$38 from the shape table entry at $808F.
$808F: shape table entry 67, the 1-pixel wide, 12-row flagpole

Books erase code $15 (3 columns by 12 rows, covering pole and flag) and draws the flagpole at base X + $71, row $2E. If the pole is off screen the base is finished. Then moves two units right for the flag itself.
the draw position triple at $0067: base X + $73, row $2E

Chooses the flag's frame from bit 0 of the frame counter $89 and reads its pointer out of $8091/$8092, shape table entries 68 and 69. The flag therefore alternates between two 11-bit by 8-row bitmaps on every frame, which is the only animation on the base.
$0065, the scratch word holding the chosen flag shape's pointer
Clips and blits the flag, the last piece of the base, and returns. No erase rectangle: the flagpole's code $15 already covers it.

The fill record for the base's apron, and the only one of its kind in the program: width 15 character columns, height 5 bitmap rows, then the four pattern bytes $AA $AA $AA $AA. $8C5E reads only those four - two for even bitmap rows, two for odd - and repeats them across the rectangle, so the apron comes out solid multicolour colour 2. It is not a shape for $8FD3 and carries no per-row bitmap. $8BBA at $BA67 hands its address to $37/$38.

Resets everything a new game starts from, called at $95B2 before the attract loop and at $95F4 when a game begins. When bit 7 of $8C is set (the status bar is wanted) it stamps the bar's fixed furniture into text row 2 of both screen matrices, $0400 and $4400: the spade, diamond and heart markers (screen codes $41, $5A, $53) at columns 8, 19 and 30, reverse vertical-bar dividers ($E5) at columns 1, 11, 22 and 33 and a closing one ($E7) at column 38, colours the marker and the two digits after it white in colour RAM ($D858, $D863, $D86E with X = 2..0), and calls $A978 three times with zero to blank the three two-digit counters. Always, it then clears the score and phase words $0CEE, $0CEF, $0CF1, $0CF2, $8D, $0CFF (the sortie number) and $0CFC..$0CFE, sets the four sheds to intact ($0CF4..$0CF7 = 0) with sixteen people inside each ($0CF8..$0CFB = $10, 64 in all), and marks all sixteen slots of the people array at $0CA0 free by writing $FF to the first byte of each 4-byte record.

Wipes the play area of both bitmap buffers before the first frame, called once at $95A5. $8CE0 resets the clip window to the full 168 rows (bottom row 0 in $3A, top row $A7 in $39) and zeroes the draw state; then, twice, $8D42 fills bitmap rows 0 to $A7 with $00 across all 40 columns and $8D16 flips the buffer select $0F, so both the $2000 and the $6000 bitmap end up blank.

Erases everything the game drew into this video buffer two frames ago, the first thing every draw sequence does ($95CB, $9651, $96A8, $9715, $9746, $9758). The game keeps two dirty-rectangle lists, $0D03 and $0DA3 set up by $A9E1, forty 4-byte records each, addressed through $99/$9A and $9B/$9C with their counts in $9D and $9E; this routine swaps the two pairs so $99 selects the list belonging to the buffer about to be drawn, walks its $9D records and clears the count. Each record, written by $AA38, is (code, screen-relative X low, X high, row). The code doubles into the size table at $94AF to give a width in character columns and a height in bitmap rows; code 0 additionally shifts the rectangle $16 left and $0E up. A rectangle hanging off the left edge has the overhang divided by 8 and taken off its width before X is clamped to 0, and one reaching above row $A7 has the overhang taken off its height before the row is clamped, which is the whole of the clipping.
the literal value $0E44 - the second and last $8BBA site; $37/$38 points at the two-byte fill header this routine has just built in RAM

Paints one dirty rectangle out. $8B91 - the fifth inline-parameter routine, alongside $8BBA, $8BE0, $8BF9 and $8C17, and called from nowhere else - takes the three bytes at $006A and puts the screen-relative X in $04/$05 and the row in $03, skipping the clipper entirely. $8C5E then fills width by height from the header at $0E44/$0E45 using the four pattern bytes at $0E46, which are zero, so the rectangle is cleared to background.
$006A: the inline pointer argument of $8B91, a fifth routine of the inline-parameter family, which loads $04/$05 and $03 from $6A/$6B/$6C
Steps to the next dirty-rectangle record, four bytes on, and loops until Y reaches the count $9D; then sets $9D to zero so this frame's $AA38 calls start refilling the same list from the beginning.

Moves the camera, the 16-bit world X in $75/$76 that every draw routine subtracts through $3B/$3C. Called once per frame at $95D1, $96B4 and $971B. Three cases. While $5F is set (the opening of a sortie) it simply adds 4 a frame and pans right. Otherwise, if the helicopter's facing $59 and the sign of its velocity high byte $52 agree - the pilot is flying the way the machine is pointing - it leads the helicopter at $BD18; if they disagree, or $5D is zero, it snaps at $BCCC: the helicopter's world X $55/$56 must stay between $46 and $FA (70 and 250) units right of the camera, and the camera is moved the minimum needed to restore that. $BD18 instead aims at the helicopter's position plus a thirty-second of its velocity, less $46 when flying left or $FA when flying right, and closes on that target by the step $BDD1 computes. Every path ends at $BD9C, which clamps the camera to $02B0..$11D8 - the edges of the world - and hands it to $8C17 to become the clip origin $3B/$3C.
$0075: the camera word, copied into the clip origin $3B/$3C
Shared exit taken when the camera is already where it should be: nothing is written and $3B/$3C keeps the value it was given last frame.

Works out how far the camera may travel this frame and leaves it in $7D. The base speed is 4 plus the magnitude of the helicopter's velocity $51/$52 divided by 256 (the signed shift $ACF1 with Y=8, then absolute value), so the view opens up as the machine accelerates. That is then capped at the distance still to go, |target - camera| from $6D/$6E, whenever the high byte of that distance is zero, so the camera never overshoots its mark.

53 bytes of 6502 code that nothing in the program references: no instruction anywhere in $8000-$BFFF names any address in $BE1D-$BE51. Read as code it is the exact mirror of the signed right shift at $ACF1 - save the sign of $7F/$80, negate if negative, asl $7F / rol $80 Y times, then negate back - that is, multiply the signed 16-bit value in $7F/$80 by 2 to the power Y. Left typed as data because nothing calls it; it looks like a routine that was written, superseded and never removed.

Sets up the world for a sortie, called once per sortie from $9618. There is no level or world table anywhere: the layout is these constants plus one use of the random source. It puts eight people on the ground ($0CF0 = 8), leaves 56 still indoors ($0CED = $38), and marks the fourth shed as already open with only eight left inside ($0CF7 = 1, $0CFB = 8 - these are element 3 of the shed-state and shed-count arrays that start at $0CF4 and $0CF8, which is why they look like lone variables). It then fills the first eight of the sixteen 4-byte records at $0CA0: field 0 is the walk-animation phase, seeded 0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3 so they do not step in time; field 1 is the walk direction, zero here so everybody starts standing; fields 2 and 3 are the 16-bit world X, starting at $0750 and advanced for each person by $20 plus a CIA1 timer sample masked with $7E ($A933), i.e. an even gap of 32 to 158 units. That spacing is the only thing that differs between one sortie and the next. The records are read and drawn by $9B7D.

Puts the helicopter back to its starting state, called at $95A8 on boot, at $95B5 when the attract loop starts and at $962C at the head of every sortie. Sets the facing $59 to 3 and the flags $8A, $5E and $5F to 1, clears $8B, $5A..$5D, $60..$64 and $0CF3, zeroes the 16-bit velocity $51/$52 and $53/$54, and places the machine at world X $1273 ($55/$56), a few units right of the base at $1254, with $57 = 7 and $58 = $16. $5F being set is what makes $BCA2 pan the camera right at 4 units a frame until the sortie proper begins. It then calls $A9E1 to rebuild the actor free list and empty both dirty-rectangle lists, selects buffer 0 with $8D0F, and runs $8D16/$8D1F/$8D16 so the VIC bank in $DD00 and the buffer-select flag $0F agree again. Finally clears $0D00.

Cold initialisation: the very first thing $959C calls, and the routine that builds every lookup table the renderer depends on. Five phases. (1) Clears $0A00-$0EFF - though the store to page $0E is coded three times over and page $0F is never cleared at all - zeroes $02 and $93 and sets the scratch fill header $0E44/$0E45 to $FF. (2) Builds the bitmap row table: $0A00,y low byte and $0AA8,y high byte, 168 entries, starting at $2500 for y = 167 and working down to $3E07 for y = 0, eight rows per character row and $0140 (320) bytes between character rows. So row index 0 is the bottom scanline of the play area and row 167 the top, and the play area begins at character row 4, just under the status bar. The second buffer is reached by exclusive-oring the high byte with $40, which is what $0F holds. (3) Builds the pre-shift tables that let shapes be plotted at any X: for each shift count n = 0..7 and each byte value y, $1000 + n*256 + y holds y >> n and $1800 + n*256 + y holds the bits pushed out of the bottom. That is 4 KB at $1000-$1FFF, RAM the VIC never sees in bank 0 because the character ROM shadows it there. (4) Copies the 2 KB character ROM from $D000 to $5000: CIA1 timer A is stopped first so no jiffy IRQ can fire while I/O is banked out, $01 is taken from $36 to $32 to expose the ROM, 8 pages are copied, $01 is restored and the timer restarted. That copy is why the status bar can use a normal character set in VIC bank 1, where the character base at VIC + $1000 is RAM at $5000. (5) Clears both bitmaps, $2000-$3FFF and $6000-$7FFF.
page $0E is cleared three times over; page $0F never is
168 bitmap rows; index 167 is built first and is the topmost
$2500, the first byte of the topmost bitmap row: bitmap base $2000 plus four character rows of 320 bytes, which is the status bar's height
build the eight pre-shift tables at $1000-$17FF and $1800-$1FFF
stop CIA1 timer A: with I/O about to be banked out a jiffy IRQ could not acknowledge itself at $DC0D
clear CHAREN: $01 goes $36 to $32, character ROM visible at $D000
destination $5000, the character base the VIC sees at bank 1 + $1000
stop after 8 pages, $5000-$57FF: the whole 2 KB character ROM
restore CHAREN, I/O back at $D000
restart CIA1 timer A
clear both bitmaps: $2000-$3FFF and $6000-$7FFF, 8 KB each
